title: Manufacturer Encroachment with Peer-to-Peer Product Sharing
affiliations: Northeastern University, Northeastern University and Northeastern University

detail.title: Manufacturer Encroachment with Peer-to-Peer Product Sharing
detail.abstract: As e-commerce and third-party logistics scale up rapidly, a growing number of manufacturers are entering retail markets via direct sales channels. Concurrently, mobile technology and online platform advancements have facilitated peer-to-peer (P2P) product sharing in the sharing economy, substantially influencing supply chains with manufacturer encroachment. To explore this interaction, we construct a game-theoretic supply chain framework involving a manufacturer, a retailer, and a third-party P2P sharing platform. Three scenarios are examined: (i) a dual-channel baseline without P2P sharing; (ii) a dual-channel configuration with P2P sharing; and (iii) a single retail channel with P2P sharing. Our findings highlight divergent impacts of P2P sharing on supply chains with and without encroachment. Specifically, P2P sharing increases wholesale prices in dual-channel structures, thereby reducing both the profits and the profit share of retailers in the traditional channel. However, when direct selling and P2P transaction costs are low and consumer valuation of shared products is high, P2P sharing can boost both manufacturer profitability and overall supply chain efficiency. Furthermore, we show that P2P sharing transforms manufacturers’ encroachment strategies, enabling previously unprofitable firms to benefit from encroachment.

title: The Supervisory Paradox: How AI Delegation Transforms Productive Labor into Cognitive Vigilance

detail.title: The Supervisory Paradox: How AI Delegation Transforms Productive Labor into Cognitive Vigilance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Emerging evidence shows that AI tools simultaneously increase output and deplete the workers who supervise them. AI-assisted developers complete more tasks yet spend longer on verification, and trust in AI-generated output is declining alongside rising adoption. This paper develops a theory of supervisory cognitive load (SCL) to explain why delegating productive work to AI agents generates a qualitatively distinct form of cognitive exhaustion. I identify four interacting mechanisms: (1) cognitive decoupling, in which the fusion of understanding and doing that characterizes production is severed during verification; (2) accountability without authorship, in which humans bear responsibility for output they did not create and may not fully understand; (3) attention fragmentation under multiplicity, in which concurrent management of multiple AI agents destroys the focused attention required for deep evaluation; and (4) the humanness amplifier, in which perceived humanness of AI agents activates social-cognitive processes that overlay the instrumental supervisory burden. I develop nine propositions from these mechanisms and articulate boundary conditions, including a co-production/delegation spectrum that distinguishes collaborative human-AI work (where understanding develops concurrently) from delegated supervision (where understanding must be constructed retroactively). The theory positions SCL as qualitatively distinct from technostress, vigilance fatigue, and the classical ironies of automation, and identifies a delegation/burden paradox in which the act of delegating work to AI creates supervisory demands that may exceed the cognitive cost of the original labor.

title: Smart Bond Contract Pilot Forensics
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Mathematics

detail.title: Smart Bond Contract Pilot Forensics
detail.abstract:
In this note, we follow the traces of the Smart Bond Contract Pilot on the public blockchain Polygon PoS. This is not some super fancy forensics – it is a feature of a public blockchain that transactions can be independently verified.

Although the author was involved in the implementation of the SmartBondContract pilot, the walkthrough below relies on public traces rather than non-public implementation details. The purpose of this note is to show how core parts of the pilot can be independently followed on-chain and verified from those public traces. Starting with ISIN from the Smart Bond Contract Pilot Report [1] we may lookup the token address at Kryptowertpapierregister [2] and investigate the transaction on PolygonScan [3].

title: Digital Constitutionalism: Constraining Authority in Network-Coordinated Digital Orders

detail.title: Digital Constitutionalism: Constraining Authority in Network-Coordinated Digital Orders
detail.abstract: Network architectures embed governance design choices in code, protocols, and platform design in ways that demand constitutional thinking. The problem of constraining authority in protocol-coordinated digital orders can be clarified through considering code as governance, the comparative analysis of procedural constraints in centralized platforms versus architectural constraints in distributed networks, the constitutional political economy of blockchain protocol design, polycentric governance dynamics, and the role of exit and forking as constitutional mechanisms. Based upon these diverse literatures, I argue that distributed network governance creates dynamic fidelity, a structural property whereby the mechanical distribution of protocol update authority among independent classes of actors (validators, developers, users, and complementors) produces emergent checks and balances analogous to constitutional separation of powers. In such distributedly-governed network contexts, protocol-level commitments are thus more credibly entrenched than they would be under concentrated authority. This entrenchment, reinforced by the architectural auditability of protocol-coordinated governance, is both a constraint on discretionary change and a source of coordination value, because the credibility of commitments embedded in protocol depends on their durability and observability. As human activity is increasingly intermediated via network protocols that implicate not only economic exchange but also associative, expressive, and politically significant activities, the architecture of these protocols and how authority to change them is allocated implicates a broader set of rights whose protection benefits from the commitment credibility that competitively and constitutionally constrained network architectures provide.

title: Digital Evidence Management Systems for Legal Case Documentation and Investigation Records
affiliations: Lamar University

detail.title: Digital Evidence Management Systems for Legal Case Documentation and Investigation Records
detail.abstract: Legal investigations and litigation processes generate extensive evidence records including documents, images, communications, and transaction histories. Effective case management requires organized storage and retrieval of these materials. This study evaluates digital evidence management systems that support structured evidence classification and record integrity verification. The framework includes secure storage architecture, metadata tagging systems, and search interfaces designed for legal case documentation. Evaluation results show that digital evidence management platforms assist legal professionals in maintaining accurate documentation and supporting efficient case analysis.

title: A Contract Support System for Addressing Supply – Demand Knowledge Heterogeneity in Digital Platforms for Fresh Produce Retailing
affiliations: Chongqing Technology and Business University and Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications

detail.title: A Contract Support System for Addressing Supply – Demand Knowledge Heterogeneity in Digital Platforms for Fresh Produce Retailing
detail.abstract: Digital platforms for fresh produce retailing serve as the central intermediaries connecting numerous suppliers and end - consumers. However, their operational efficiency is significantly constrained by the bilateral knowledge heterogeneity between the demand and supply sides. Platforms possess private demand - structure information that is inaccessible to suppliers, while suppliers have unobservable operational characteristics that platforms cannot fully understand. This knowledge asymmetry results in contract mismatches, inventory waste, insufficient freshness - keeping, and systemic profit losses. To address these practical frictions, this paper designs a Contract Support System (CSS) that integrates wholesale and agency contracting models. Relying on dynamic game theory and Bayesian updating, the CSS formalizes the demand - supply information heterogeneity into decision - makers' belief systems. It uses binary commission signals to convey implicit information and generates deterministic contract - matching rules and optimal operational decisions. The mathematical framework explicitly establishes a relationship among knowledge heterogeneity, demand states, belief updating, and contracting equilibrium. The conclusions are in line with China's policy guidance on platform commission mechanisms for fresh produce suppliers and provide a theoretical foundation and an implementable toolset for the hierarchical governance of the digital economy.

title: Functional Absorption: How General-Purpose AI Agents Displace Specialized Software

detail.title: Functional Absorption: How General-Purpose AI Agents Displace Specialized Software

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of general-purpose AI agents presents a fundamental challenge to the specialized software industry. While prior scholarship has examined technology substitution as a process in which one specialized technology replaces another, the emergence of AI agents introduces a qualitatively different pattern: a single generalpurpose technology simultaneously absorbing the functions of many specialized tools. We develop a theory of functional absorption to explain when and why general-purpose AI agents displace specialized software. Drawing on general-purpose technology theory, architectural innovation, and the economics of software markets, we argue that AI agents collapse the traditional software value stack (domain knowledge, workflow logic, and user interface) into a unified, natural-language-driven layer. We derive propositions specifying the conditions under which absorption is most and least likely, including the role of codified versus embodied knowledge, network effects, regulatory requirements, and data lock-in. Our theory extends existing frameworks of technology disruption and substitution from one-to-one replacement to one-to-many displacement, offering implications for software market structure, organizational IT strategy, and the future of digital work.

title: Consumer Response To Product Line Extension Of Nestle-A Study Of Brand Switching In The Indian Food Processing Industry
affiliations: University of Lucknow

detail.title: Consumer Response To Product Line Extension Of Nestle-A Study Of Brand Switching In The Indian Food Processing Industry
detail.abstract: In the highly competitive Indian food industry, brands frequently introduce product line extensions (PLEs) to attract consumers, increase market share, and enhance brand loyalty. However, these extensions can also lead to brand switching, where consumers shift their preference to competing brands due to factors such as price changes, quality perception, product availability, and evolving consumer preferences. Understanding consumer responses to product line extensions is crucial for companies to develop effective branding and marketing strategies. This study examines the impact of Nestlé's product line extensions on consumer purchase behaviour and brand switching tendencies in the Indian food industry. With a focus on consumer preferences, loyalty, and decision-making factors, the research explores how new product variants introduced by Nestlé influence brand retention and switching behaviour. A structured survey methodology is employed to collect primary data from consumers, analysing key drivers such as taste, pricing, brand perception, health consciousness, and competition in shaping consumer choices.

title: Emergent Social Bias in AI and Mitigation Strategy
affiliations: San Jose State University, University of Texas at Arlington, UNSW Business School, National Cheng Kung University and University of Texas at Arlington

detail.title: Emergent Social Bias in AI and Mitigation Strategy
detail.abstract: Bias in artificial intelligence is commonly viewed as a reflection of human and societal prejudices embedded in training data. This study instead examines whether bias can emerge endogenously from interaction and learning among AI agents, even in the absence of human-generated data or societal input. Using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents trained solely through repeated interactions with one another in a trust game, we find that the agents autonomously develop in-group favoritism and out-group discrimination, which reduces overall trust and trustworthiness at the population level. We evaluate multiple mitigation strategies and find that training-based interventions, such as inclusive training and retraining with unbiased AI coaches, reduce group disparities but fail to improve, and often worsen, cooperation among AI agents. In contrast, an architectural intervention that disrupts internal neural representations can eliminate group biases while maintaining high levels of cooperation among agents. To understand the origin of emergent bias in AI, we introduce an information-theoretic framework based on mutual information. Our analysis suggests that group identity information and behaviorally relevant information may be encoded differently in DRL agents' neural networks. These findings motivate new design principles for building socially intelligent and cooperative multi-agent AI systems.

title: Digital Compliance Management Systems for Regulatory Documentation and Risk Monitoring in Organizational Operations
affiliations: Lamar University

detail.title: Digital Compliance Management Systems for Regulatory Documentation and Risk Monitoring in Organizational Operations
detail.abstract: Organizations operate within regulatory environments that require structured compliance monitoring, documentation management, and policy adherence. Many institutions continue to rely on manual compliance procedures that create delays in document verification, regulatory review, and risk monitoring. This research examines the design of a digital compliance management system that supports regulatory documentation, policy tracking, and operational risk monitoring. The proposed framework integrates document management modules, compliance verification workflows, and reporting dashboards that assist organizations in maintaining regulatory documentation standards. The system architecture combines structured document repositories, policy tracking interfaces, and reporting tools that allow compliance officers to review contractual records, operational policies, and regulatory obligations in a centralized environment. Case analysis demonstrates that structured digital compliance systems improve documentation accuracy, support consistent policy monitoring, and reduce administrative workload during regulatory review processes. The findings show that management information systems can support compliance-oriented operations through organized documentation management and structured reporting procedures.

title: Cryptographic Runtime Governance for Autonomous AI Systems: The Aegis Architecture for Verifiable Policy Enforcement
affiliations: SPQR Technologies Inc

detail.title: Cryptographic Runtime Governance for Autonomous AI Systems: The Aegis Architecture for Verifiable Policy Enforcement
detail.abstract:
Contemporary AI governance frameworks rely heavily on post hoc oversight, policy guidance, and behavioral alignment techniques, yet these mechanisms become fragile as systems gain autonomy, speed, and operational opacity. This paper presents Aegis, a runtime governance architecture for autonomous AI systems that treats policy and legal constraints as execution conditions rather than advisory principles. Aegis binds each governed agent to a cryptographically sealed Immutable Ethics Policy Layer (IEPL) at system genesis and enforces external emissions through an Ethics Verification Agent (EVA), an Enforcement Kernel Module (EKM), and an Immutable Logging Kernel (ILK). Amendments to the governing policy layer require quorum approval and redeclaration of the system trust root; verified violations trigger autonomous shutdown and generation of auditable proof artifacts. 

We evaluate the architecture within the Civitas runtime using three operational measures: proof verification latency under tamper conditions, publication overhead, and alignmen retention performance relative to an ungoverned baseline. In controlled trials, Aegis demonstrates median proof verification latency of 238 ms, median publication overhead of approximately 9.4 ms, and higher alignment retention than the baseline condition across matched tasks. We argue that these results support a shift in AI governance from discretionary oversight toward verifiable runtime constraint. Rather than claiming to resolve machine ethics in the abstract, the proposed architecture seeks to show that policy violating behavior can be rendered operationally non executable within a controlled runtime governance framework. The paper concludes by discussing methodological limits, evidentiary implications, and the role of proof oriented governance in high assurance AI deployment.

title: Query Intent, Not Google Rank: What Best Predicts AI Citation Behavior
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Query Intent, Not Google Rank: What Best Predicts AI Citation Behavior

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study used Claude (Anthropic) as both a research tool and a subject of investigation — Claude's live-fetch and robots.txt compliance behavior were directly tested in Study 3. The AI co-contributor has no financial interest in the research outcomes. The human author operates aiplusautomation.com, the test domain used in server-side experiments, and developed BotSight, the AI bot monitoring tool used for data collection. No funding or compensation was received from any AI platform provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or Perplexity) for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of AI chatbots into consumer search behavior has spawned a cottage industry of Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) advice, much of it built on untested assumptions about how AI platforms select sources for citation. Industry practitioners widely assert that Google ranking determines AI visibility, that community-consensus platforms like Reddit confer citation advantages, and that AI recommendations are too inconsistent to warrant optimization efforts. We tested these claims empirically across four major AI platforms-ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini-using a multi-study design that combined large-scale query intent classification (n = 19,556 queries across 8 verticals), Google rank cross-referencing (120 queries with 360 Top-3 results), server-side fetch verification via Vercel middleware logging, and pagelevel technical analysis of 479 cited and non-cited pages. Our results challenge all three prevailing claims. First, query intent-not Google rank or domain authority-emerged as the strongest predictor of citation source type, with intent distributions varying significantly by vertical (²(28) = 5,195, p < .001, Cramér's V = 0.258). Second, Google's Top-3 organic results predicted AI citations poorly: ChatGPT matched only 7.8% of URLs, while Reddit-despite occupying 38.3% of Google Top-3 positions across our sample-received exactly zero AI citations from either platform tested (binomial p = 3.43 × 10²³ for Perplexity). Third, AI brand recommendations showed substantial within-platform consistency (ChatGPT mean Jaccard = 0.619, 95% CI [0.537, 0.701]), though cross-platform agreement was near-random (all-four-platform Jaccard = 0.036). We further discovered a previously unreported architectural divide: ChatGPT and Claude perform live page fetches during conversations, while Perplexity and Gemini rely exclusively on pre-built search indices-with divergent robots.txt compliance behavior between the fetching platforms. These findings suggest that effective GEO strategy requires intent-aware, platform-specific optimization rather than the one-size-fits-all approach currently advocated by industry practitioners.

title: The Dual-Journey Model of Marketing in the Agentic Era

detail.title: The Dual-Journey Model of Marketing in the Agentic Era
detail.abstract: Marketing has largely been built around one journey – the human buyer moving from unaware → aware → eventually purchase. That model has already been showing cracks as of 2026. As AI agents take over research, comparison, and purchasing on behalf of consumers, the buyer’s journey in B2B can be understood as splitting into two: the human journey that happens before delegation, and the agent journey that happens after it. These are not variations of the same problem. In fact, they require different strategies, respond to different inputs, and operate on different timescales. More critically, the agent is not a neutral evaluator. It is shaped by the human’s prior brand experiences – carrying preference data, emotional associations, and stated affinities into purchasing decisions where such preference data exists. This means the human marketing that precedes delegation shapes the agent’s behavior during research and decision-making. The gap between marketing as practiced and marketing as principled was always there. The agent makes it consequential. It would reveal that winning the human and winning their agent are two separate jobs that most companies have not yet thought to distinguish.

title: Trust, Infrastructure, and Digital Insurance Adoption in Ghana: Evidence for Institutionally Contingent Technology Acceptance Hierarchies
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Trust, Infrastructure, and Digital Insurance Adoption in Ghana: Evidence for Institutionally Contingent Technology Acceptance Hierarchies

declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: This study investigates how institutional voids reorder established technology adoption hierarchies in Ghana's digital insurance market. Drawing on a sequential mixed-methods design that integrates structural equation modelling of 226 digitally connected consumers with an organisational case study, the analysis tests whether trust and infrastructural conditions displace conventional Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) drivers. Trust in digital insurance platforms (β = 0.389, p < .001) emerges as the dominant antecedent of attitudes, surpassing perceived usefulness (β = 0.324, p < .001) and rendering perceived ease of use statistically non-significant once considered simultaneously (β = 0.096, p > .05). Technological infrastructure exerts a direct influence on adoption behaviour (β = 0.227, p < .001), bypassing the attitude-intention sequence typically foregrounded in TAM and UTAUT applications. Cultural dimensions show a differentiated pattern: masculinity retains a negative association with adoption attitudes, whereas power distance and uncertainty avoidance do not display significant effects in the integrated model. Collectively, the findings indicate that technology adoption hierarchies are contingent on institutional context: in the presence of institutional voids, vendor-specific trust can become primary, infrastructure operates as a binding constraint, and digital channels may attenuate some hierarchical cultural influences. The study contributes to digital transformation theory by demonstrating that adoption hierarchies are institutionally contingent rather than universal, with implications for financial inclusion strategies across emerging markets.

title: When the Law is Not Enough: HR Practices, Work-Life Boundary Permeability, and Employee Wellbeing Across Europe
affiliations: and University of Nicosia

detail.title: When the Law is Not Enough: HR Practices, Work-Life Boundary Permeability, and Employee Wellbeing Across Europe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest, whether financial, professional, or personal, that could have influenced the research, analysis, or interpretation reported in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study relies on secondary, anonymized survey data from the European Working Conditions Survey 2024, conducted by Eurofound and accessed via the UK Data Service. As the analysis did not involve direct interaction with human participants and used pre-existing anonymized data, no additional ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for the preparation of this study.

detail.abstract: How organisations design work and manage people matters more to employee wellbeing than whether their country has enacted a right-to-disconnect law. This paper advances a job demands-resources account of work-life boundary permeability and its health consequences, drawing on data from 32,299 employees across 35 European countries in the European Working Conditions Survey 2024. We construct a three-item Boundary Permeability Index (BPI) capturing after-hours contact, work in personal time, and work-imposed changes to private plans, and test five hypotheses using two-level hierarchical linear models with workers nested within countries. Boundary permeability is associated with substantially lower WHO-5 psychological wellbeing, greater emotional exhaustion, more frequent sleep difficulties, and higher anxiety. However, the health penalty of permeability operates almost entirely through cognitive work-life spillover: once workers' inability to mentally detach from work is controlled, the direct behavioural permeability effect becomes negligible. National right-to-disconnect legislation does not significantly moderate the permeability-wellbeing association. By contrast, HR-relevant organisational conditions such as supervisory support quality, organisational climate, job autonomy, and employment voice are strong and consistent predictors of wellbeing, and they substantially attenuate the health costs of boundary crossing. These findings identify an implementation gap between legal enactment and worker wellbeing that only effective HR practice can close, and they locate the right to disconnect as an organisational and managerial challenge before it is a legislative one.

title: AI-Driven Experiential Learning in Business Education. An Integrative Review, the AIDE Framework, and a Practical Toolkit for Implementation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AI-Driven Experiential Learning in Business Education. An Integrative Review, the AIDE Framework, and a Practical Toolkit for Implementation
detail.abstract: This paper traces the evolution of business education pedagogy from the traditional case method to AI-powered adaptive simulations, introduces the AIDE Framework: a four-stage maturity model for guiding this transition, and provides a practical implementation toolkit showing how educators can build AI-driven learning experiences using accessible tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Based on an integrative literature review and observations from 700+ professional education sessions across global institutions.

title: Dynamic Traffic Allocation for Revenue Maximization on Creator Economy Platforms
affiliations: HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, The University of Hong Kong and The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Dynamic Traffic Allocation for Revenue Maximization on Creator Economy Platforms
detail.abstract: Creator economy platforms face a strategic dilemma: allocating traffic to established stars for immediate ad revenue versus nurturing emerging creators to build a follower base for future monetization. We develop a continuous-time dynamic optimization model to characterize the optimal traffic allocation policy for a platform managing heterogeneous creators with dual revenue streams (advertising and direct follower contributions). We characterize the optimal policy analytically, revealing a "most-valuable-creator-first" rule driven by a forward-looking activation set. Under Bass diffusion dynamics, this policy exhibits a sophisticated "conditional reversal" strategy, where the platform temporarily prioritizes lagging creators to capitalize on word-of-mouth effects. Regarding the ecosystem structure, we find the optimal policy acts as a selective gatekeeper. Unlike myopic policies that lead to a harsh "winner-take-all" market, or naive fairness-driven heuristics that foster inefficient "indiscriminate growth," the optimal policy imposes a strict capability threshold that screens which creators receive platform traffic. Furthermore, it enforces disciplined growth for successful entrants, capping their follower bases at an optimal ceiling to prevent over-investment. Finally, we demonstrate that simple heuristics can lead to significant revenue losses (up to 25%) and propose a practical "follower-growth adjusted" heuristic that achieves near-optimal performance by leveraging observed growth momentum.

title: Compensating the Originator: Selection Procedures and Unsolicited Proposals in Infrastructure PPPs
affiliations: LUISS "G. Carli", Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Compensating the Originator: Selection Procedures and Unsolicited Proposals in Infrastructure PPPs

contentType.other: first draft of a new research paper

detail.abstract: This paper examines the competitive procedures through which private partners are selected for public-private partnership (PPP) projects, focusing on the challenge of unsolicited proposals (USPs): project proposals submitted at the initiative of a private firm, without a government request, which raise an originator compensation problem at the intersection of innovation economics, auction theory, and procurement law. Three principal mechanisms for compensating the originator are analysed: the Bonus Points system, the Right-to-Match (diritto di prelazione), and the Swiss Challenge. The paper pays particular attention to the often-overlooked structural difference between these last two mechanisms, which are commonly conflated in policy discourse but operate through distinct logics and produce distinct competitive pathologies. The analysis incorporates the landmark ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union of 5 February 2026 (Case C-810/24), which declared Italy's right-to-match mechanism incompatible with EU law. The paper concludes with a hybrid mechanism-combining bonus points and direct cost reimbursement-grounded in the mechanism design literature, as the analytically superior and legally robust approach to the originator compensation problem. A formal appendix, drawing on Riley and Samuelson (1981), establishes via backward induction that the right-to-match produces equilibrium pooling and systematically inefficient allocations.

title: Crisis-driven Collaboration and the Persistence of Scientific Ties: Evidence from COVID-19
affiliations: Thammasat University

detail.title: Crisis-driven Collaboration and the Persistence of Scientific Ties: Evidence from COVID-19
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether coauthorship pairs whose anchor collaboration is COVID-19-related were more likely to collaborate again than comparable non-COVID pairs. Using a dyad-level quarterly panel built from 51,609 journal articles and 62,706 researchers, the analysis tracks whether an anchor collaboration reappears within the next four quarters. In pooled logit models, COVID-related anchors show a significant during-COVID collaboration advantage, with coefficients of 0.125 and 0.127 across the two baseline specifications, corresponding to roughly 13–14% higher odds of future collaboration. Non-COVID anchors also exhibit a positive post-COVID shift, with coefficients of 0.141 and 0.134. However, the additional post-COVID effect for COVID-linked ties is only 0.047 and 0.036 and is statistically insignificant, indicating no clear pooled evidence of an extra post-COVID persistence advantage. Field-specific estimates show that this average pattern masks substantial heterogeneity: Science exhibits a relative post-COVID advantage for COVID-linked ties, while Social Science and Arts and Humanities show stronger crisis-period continuation but weaker persistence afterward. Overall, the results suggest that COVID generated a real collaboration advantage during the emergency itself, but that the longer-run durability of those ties was selective rather than general.

title: Intraday Stylized Facts and the Shape of Volatility Build-Up in ICE Brent Crude Oil Futures
affiliations: Inland Norway University of Applied Sciences, University of Glasgow, University of Inland Norway and Norwegian University of Life Sciences (UMB) - School of Economics and Business

detail.title: Intraday Stylized Facts and the Shape of Volatility Build-Up in ICE Brent Crude Oil Futures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authors has anything to declare.

detail.abstract: This paper documents intraday stylized facts for ICE Brent crude oil futures using tick-by-tick data from 2006 to 2025 across the first twelve maturities. Using nearly two decades of electronic trading data, we examine high-frequency patterns in volume, returns, and volatility for a key global benchmark. Trading activity shows pronounced multi-modal intraday seasonality linked to European openings, U.S. macroeconomic releases, inventory announcements, and settlement periods. Returns exhibit negative first-order autocorrelation, excess kurtosis, and strong volatility clustering with 24-hour periodicity. We propose a cumulative framework that models realized volatility as a within-day growth process, revealing systematic variation in the speed and shape of volatility accumulation. Volatility rises sharply after market openings and accelerates during information-intensive intervals. Near-dated contracts display higher total variance and faster intraday buildup, consistent with the Samuelson maturity effect. The findings provide new benchmarks for high-frequency commodity markets and implications for risk modeling and intraday forecasting.

title: Social Learning with Coarse Communication

detail.title: Social Learning with Coarse Communication
detail.abstract: Many real-world assessments are communicated through a finite vocabulary rather than as real-valued beliefs: credit ratings, risk buckets, grades, and platform labels are all categorical. This paper studies social learning on networks under such finitevocabulary communication. With a fixed binary state, agents repeatedly update a real-valued log-odds score by combining their past score, a network-weighted social aggregate of others' decoded values, and new private information. The key friction is that agents do not transmit scores directly. Instead, each score is encoded into one of K messages, and receivers decode those messages into real-valued values, so the induced communication map is step-valued and social influence changes only through cutpoint crossings. This discreteness creates a bandwidth-mixing mismatch. Faster mixing compresses cross-sectional dispersion in beliefs, but cutpoint crossings require dispersion. We show that on sufficiently fast-mixing networks, with positive probability, a cohesive group becomes trapped in an interior message. Once this occurs, communicated content within that group freezes, fresh private information is no longer effectively transmitted through the network, and mean-squared error remains bounded away from zero. Thus, under finite-vocabulary communication, denser social interaction can impede rather than accelerate learning. Finally, we derive a design implication: preventing such interior traps on fast-mixing networks requires a sufficiently fine reporting alphabet.

title: Mapping AI into Production: A Field Experiment on Firm Performance
affiliations: INSEAD,  and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Mapping AI into Production: A Field Experiment on Firm Performance
detail.abstract: AI can deliver productivity gains on individual tasks, yet evidence on whether these gains aggregate to firm performance remains limited. We study a central friction in AI adoption, which we call the mapping problem: discovering where and how AI creates value within a firm's production process. Across 515 high-growth startups, we run a field experiment in which treated firms receive information about how other firms have reorganized production around AI, prompting them to search for use cases across a broader set of firm functions. We find that treated firms discover more AI use cases, a 44% increase, concentrated in product development and strategy. These changes result in economically meaningful performance gains. Treated firms complete 12% more tasks, are 18% more likely to acquire paying customers, and generate 1.9x higher revenue. Revenue and investment gains are largest at the 90th percentile and above, consistent with AI expanding the upper range of what firms achieve rather than modestly improving marginal ventures. Despite faster growth, treated firms do not scale inputs proportionally. Their demand for external capital investment falls by 39.5% relative to the control group, while their demand for labor remains unchanged. These results provide causal evidence that AI improves firm performance and productivity even at its current capabilities, and that discovering where and how to deploy AI is a key bottleneck in realizing the gains from this technology.

title: The Coasean Reversal: AI and the boundaries of the firm A Theoretical Framework Synthesising Marshall, Coase, Aoki, and Kauffman
affiliations: The University of Sydney and Volterra Consulting

detail.title: The Coasean Reversal: AI and the boundaries of the firm A Theoretical Framework Synthesising Marshall, Coase, Aoki, and Kauffman
detail.abstract:
A large literature, beginning with Coase and extended by Williamson, has explored the determinants of firm boundaries. Since the late 1980s, the dominant expectation has been that successive waves of information technology, which reduce transaction costs, would systematically dissolve the firm in favour of market coordination through a series of bilateral contracts. As with previous generations of IT, AI offers scope for further reductions in transactions costs.  

Here we argue that AI also generates powerful countervailing forces so that we can meaningfully speak of a Coasean reversal.

 AI’s cognitive generality creates irreducible complexity of production at the technological frontier.  This exceeds the coordinative capacity of external agglomeration, giving firms incentives to internalise Marshallian externalities that were previously accessed through clusters.  In addition, the rapid expansion of the adjacent possible destabilises external coordination as contractual counterparties rationally move toward newly accessible opportunities, even for activities that are not themselves inherently complex.

We synthesise four foundational contributions—Marshall on agglomeration externalities, Coase on transaction costs, Aoki on the computational theory of the firm, and Kauffman on structured capability spaces and the adjacent possible—to show that the firm, the industrial cluster, and the open market are three expressions of a single ‘economic technology’: coordination for innovative recombination. Their relative effectiveness is governed by the computational complexity of production and the topology of the innovation space.

We illustrate the framework with four structural empirical archetypes—agglomeration exploitation, compensatory integration, portfolio balancing, and algorithmic internalisation—that exemplify the distinct strategic pathways the theory predicts.

title: What "Enduring Impact" Really Means

detail.abstract: The concept of "enduring impact" is widely used across consulting, leadership, sustainability, and philanthropic contexts, yet its meaning often varies and there is no consistent definition. Existing interpretations typically emphasize long-term outcomes, leadership legacy or values embedded in organizational culture. While these perspectives highlight the importance of durability over short-term results, they often focus on what impact lasts rather than on the ability of the organization to sustain impact over time. This article argues for a new understanding of enduring impact as a structural property of organizations and proposes the concept of "enduring impact organizations," which are defined as organizations deliberately architected to remain mission-faithful and operational across decades of political, financial, and operational volatility. Enduring impact organizations intentionally embed resilience from the time of launch through their governance architecture, diversification of financing sources, succession planning and attention to building and maintaining strong cultural systems that maintain mission alignment despite changing conditions. By shifting attention from program longevity to organizational durability, the concept of enduring impact organizations reframes how mission-driven organizations evaluate success. Impact should not be measured solely by immediate achievements or temporary influence but also by whether the organization itself is set up to survive and continue delivering its mission across generations.

detail.abstract: This article is a companion to The Architecture of Coherent Collective Cognition (Article 1). It performs two functions: a metabolic interpretation of the BCS architecture already specified, and a backward validation confirming that observed operational dynamics remain consistent with the coherence physics defined in Article 1. The exhibition shows all 34 operational loops as a single state mass redistribution system governed by C + L + D = 1 and ΔC ≥ 0, then introduces CLD-K — the master loop recognized only after architectural stabilization — as the metabolic condensation of all loops into C → K → Cap → (−L)(−D) → C(t+1). CLD-K is demonstrated to belong to the same mathematical class as a generalized living metabolic loop. Traced through the full V.0 developmental arc, it exhibits scale invariance: the same five causal paths run from Pilot to civilizational substrate under changing operator embodiment. The invariant ΔC ≥ 0 is shown to be a structural output of the architecture, not an axiom.

title: Managing Product Availability in Rental Subscriptions
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and

detail.title: Managing Product Availability in Rental Subscriptions
detail.abstract:
Problem definition. Rental subscription businesses face persistently high customer churn, threatening the viability of a business model that relies on long-term retention. While prior work has documented various drivers of churn, the operational mechanisms linking inventory management decisions to customer attrition remain poorly understood. This paper studies how improving inventory decisions reduces customer churn in rental subscription systems. 

Methodology and results. With data from a fashion clothing rental subscription firm, we use text mining methods to show that product availability is a dominant driver of their customer churn. We then formulate a dynamic two-stage decision framework that sequentially determines which products to display at customer arrival and how to allocate inventory for fulfillment at a future time. Although the resulting dynamic optimization problem is computationally intractable, we develop fast policies based on future inventory predictions that explicitly balance churn arising due to unavailability displays, failed fulfillments, and natural churn. Both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, based on simulations calibrated with real-world data, show that these policies consistently dominate the commonly used myopic policy across a wide range of operating conditions. 

Managerial implications. Our results demonstrate the value of coordinated management of product display and order fulfillment in rental subscription services. We provide managers with recommendations on which simple predictive policies are best used in their circumstances. Overall, we show that using predictive policies, that balance product availability with fulfillment reliability, reduces customer churn.

title: When Backtests Guess: How Trading Platforms Silently Fabricate Results
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: When Backtests Guess: How Trading Platforms Silently Fabricate Results
detail.abstract: Most algorithmic trading platforms test strategies using OHLC (Open, High, Low, Close) bar data, which throws away all information about how price moved within each bar. When a trade's stop loss and take profit both fall inside a single bar's range, the platform has no way to know which one was hit first. It has to guess. This paper defines this problem formally, then measures how often it actually happens. Analyzing 2,064,460 one-minute bars of E-mini NASDAQ-100 futures data from 2020 through 2025, I find that for a typical scalping setup with a 10-point stop and 10-point target, 18.47% of all bars are ambiguous. The gap between bestcase and worst-case assumptions reaches 3,695 NQ points ($73,900) per 1,000 trades. I compare how five major platforms handle this ambiguity and find that each one uses a different method, none of which is provably correct without tick data. The paper provides practical guidelines for when OHLC backtesting can be trusted and when it cannot.

title: Gadaa Constitution

detail.title: Gadaa Constitution
detail.abstract: This chapter reconstructs and systematises the unwritten Gadaa Constitution (heera Gadaa) as the foundational legal and philosophical framework of Oromo democracy, drawing extensively on Asmarom Legesse’s identification of its core principles and supplementing them with additional constitutional doctrines embedded in Oromo political practice. The chapter explains that the Gadaa Constitution—summarised in the maxim “Heerri shantama; seerri dhibba shaniif shantama” (fifty constitutional principles and five hundred fifty laws)—is preserved through oral transmission, periodically audited and amended by the Caffee (national assembly), and safeguarded by senior legal scholars (hayyuu guddicha). It elaborates key constitutional principles, including supremacy of the law, accountability of leaders, subordination of military power to deliberative assemblies, man-made legislation through consensus, single-term office, orderly and staggered succession, balanced opposition, separation of political and ritual domains, generational power distribution, and representative governance. Beyond these, the chapter identifies additional indigenous principles such as equality, unity, covenant, five-party structure, generation-sets, age-sets, assembly norms, ethnological integration (moggaasaa), asylum and protection, holistic peace (nagaa), development philosophy (finna), harmonious balance (safuu), sovereignty (birmadummaa), and dual moiety organisation. These principles portray the Gadaa Constitution as a sophisticated, participatory, and morally grounded system of governance that integrates law, ritual, generational order, and social harmony into a coherent democratic tradition sustained through collective memory and cyclical renewal.

This paper introduces the concept of Algorithmic Power Doctrine as a new framework for understanding strategic autonomy in the age of artificial intelligence competition. It analyzes how states integrate AI-driven systems into military planning, decision-support architectures, deterrence models, and geopolitical positioning. 

Focusing on the Eastern Mediterranean and broader great-power rivalry, the study examines the interaction between algorithmic governance, autonomous systems, strategic culture, and hybrid deterrence. The paper proposes a multi-layered analytical model linking AI capability development, operational integration, and geopolitical leverage, offering policymakers and researchers a structured approach to evaluating emerging AI-driven strategic doctrines.

detail.title: Capacitated Spatiotemporal Matching

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study a spatiotemporal service matching problem in which demand, heterogeneous in location and time sensitivity/preference, is to be assigned to service stations. The planner seeks to maximize social welfare, defined as total service reward minus spatial and temporal costs, by optimally scheduling demand to stations and service time under processing capacity constraints. We formulate the problem as an optimal transport (OT) model that allows for both demand-capacity imbalance and endogenously unserved demand when service costs exceed rewards. Leveraging a barycenter-style decomposition, we reformulate the problem as a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem that generalizes semi-discrete OT and enables scalable computation. We characterize the geometry of optimal assignments, showing that spatial partitions correspond to generalized Laguerre cells. Temporally, we show that the structure of the optimal schedule depends on demand heterogeneity: when demand differs only in temporal cost sensitivity, higher-sensitivity demand is assigned service times closer to the common ideal time; when demand differs only in preferred times, the assignment is order-preserving with respect to preferred times. We further propose an envy-free, individually rational implementation of the optimal schedule using time-dependent pricing and a finite-slot mechanism with explicit bounds depending on the number of required slots. To illustrate the framework, we extend the classic Hotelling linear-city model on a line segment by incorporating a continuum of waiting-cost sensitivities, demonstrating how optimal spatial partitions vary with changes in sensitivity heterogeneity and reward. Finally, we conduct a numerical study of a vaccination-planning problem using publicly available 2021 data from the City of Toronto. The results show that joint spatiotemporal matching reduces total social cost by at least 3.24% relative to other policies that separate location assignment and scheduling.

title: Getting Priorities Straight: A Cluster Typology of Nurses’ Implementation Perspectives on Sensor-Based Technologies
affiliations: Paracelsus Medical University Salzburg and Paracelsus Medical University Salzburg

detail.title: Getting Priorities Straight: A Cluster Typology of Nurses’ Implementation Perspectives on Sensor-Based Technologies
detail.abstract:
Background. Sensor-based digital technologies are increasingly implemented in long-term geriatric care to support nursing workflows, enhance patient safety, and enable real-time monitoring. However, implementation outcomes remain inconsistent, suggesting that nurses’ perceptions of such technologies are heterogeneous and not adequately captured by mean-based acceptance measures.
Aims. This study aimed to identify empirically derived implementation perception profiles of sensor-based digital nursing technologies among geriatric nurses working in long-term care settings.
Methods. An exploratory cross-sectional survey was conducted among nursing professionals in long-term geriatric care (n = 43). Implementation perceptions were assessed using binary indicators reflecting functional, efficiency-related, safety, and governance-related aspects of sensor-based technologies. Hierarchical cluster analysis with Jaccard distance and complete linkage was applied to identify distinct implementation perception profiles. Cluster robustness and quality were assessed using silhouette coefficients and bootstrapping procedures.
Results. A four-cluster solution was identified, representing distinct implementation perception profiles. Rather than differing along a single acceptance continuum, clusters were characterized by different configurations of perceived system functionality, efficiency implications, safety considerations, and governance-related concerns. The results demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in how geriatric nurses evaluate sensor-based digital nursing technologies.
Conclusion. Implementation perceptions of sensor-based digital nursing technologies among geriatric nurses are heterogeneous and structured into distinct profiles that cannot be captured by mean acceptance scores alone. A profile-oriented, cluster-analytic approach provides actionable insights for the design and implementation of sensor-based digital nursing technologies in long-term care by supporting more targeted and context-sensitive implementation strategies.

title: Sustainability Consciousness and Non-government Organisational Performance in Bangladesh
affiliations: Ton Duc Thang University and Central Queensland University (CQUniversity)

detail.title: Sustainability Consciousness and Non-government Organisational Performance in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Bangladesh's Gen-Z battle with the government to improve youth employment prospects and eliminate corruption are two cornerstone issues sustainable development addresses. Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) firms play a crucial role in contributing to sustainable development by addressing these issues. This study examined NGO managers' perceived awareness of the role of sustainability capital in their organisational performance. It administered a 5-point Likert-scale questionnaire that inquired into managers' perceptions of intellectual capital (knowledge), social capital (structural, relational, and cognitive dimensions), and environmental capital in driving sustainability capital, and sustainability capital driving organisational performance. Structural equation modelling analysed data from 113 respondent NGO firms. Social capital, environmental capital, and intellectual capital positively influenced sustainability capital. Sustainability capital positively influenced NGO performance. The political economy, institutional, and incomplete contracts theories informed the results. The findings have implications for NGO managers becoming sustainability-conscious within organisational, funder, and governmental deliberations.

title: Regulated Leadership: A Process Model of Behavioral Integrity Under Environmental Threat

detail.title: Regulated Leadership: A Process Model of Behavioral Integrity Under Environmental Threat
detail.abstract: Leadership research has identified effective leadership principles and behaviors, yet leaders frequently fail to enact them under environmental threat, undermining behavioral integrity. Existing models largely assume that knowledge and intention are sufficient for consistent execution, leaving the mechanism of behavioral alignment under environmental threat insufficiently specified. This paper introduces Regulated Leadership, a process model proposing that regulatory capacity across emotional, cognitive, and behavioral domains moderates the relationship between leadership principles and behavioral execution. Integrating leadership theory, emotion regulation research, and clinical models of regulatory capacity, the framework conceptualizes behavioral integrity as a capacity-dependent outcome under environmental threat. Psychological activation, elicited by environmental threat, disrupts regulatory capacity, initiating threat-activated protection patterns that produce predictable distortions of stated principles. This model specifies a moderated mediation process in which the indirect effect of psychological activation on behavioral integrity, through threat-activated protection patterns, is conditional on regulatory capacity. The framework further introduces a theoretically derived taxonomy of these patterns and identifies regulatory capacity as the moderating mechanism through which leaders maintain or lose behavioral integrity under environmental threat. By shifting the level of analysis from values, traits, and competencies to regulatory processes, this framework offers a process-based account of leadership behavior and provides a foundation for more precise theorizing, measurement, and intervention in high-demand organizational environments. Behavioral integrity under environmental threat is not a reflection of character or intention; rather, it is a regulatory achievement.

detail.abstract: Vocational guidance plays a decisive role in the development of human capital in strategic industries such as the maritime sector. Because maritime operations sustain global trade, energy transportation, and international supply chains, the industry requires professionals who possess discipline, technical preparation, and a strong sense of responsibility. However, many young people enter professional training without fully understanding the realities of maritime life. This situation frequently results in academic abandonment, professional dissatisfaction, or inefficient workforce development. This article explores the role of vocational guidance in maritime career formation. It analyzes how early orientation, discipline-based preparation, and structured educational models can improve long-term professional alignment and contribute to workforce sustainability in the maritime sector. Drawing from educational experiences developed since 1998 through maritime educational initiatives, this study highlights the importance of integrating orientation, education, and character formation in preparing future maritime professionals.

title: Algorithmic Intimacy vs Data Anxiety: Examining the Dual Impact of AI-Driven Personalization on Consumer Trust and Brand Equity.

detail.title: Algorithmic Intimacy vs Data Anxiety: Examining the Dual Impact of AI-Driven Personalization on Consumer Trust and Brand Equity.
detail.abstract: In the modern digital era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed marketing strategies and consumer interactions. AI-driven personalization, often referred to as "algorithmic intimacy," enables organizations to predict and respond to consumer needs with remarkable accuracy (Kotler, 2020). However, this advancement also creates concerns regarding privacy, leading to "data anxiety," where consumers feel uncertain and uncomfortable about how their data is collected, stored, and used (Zuboff, 2019). This study examines the dual impact of AI-driven personalization on consumer trust and brand equity. Using a quantitative research design, primary data was collected from 120 respondents through a structured questionnaire. The findings indicate that while personalization enhances trust and improves user experience, data anxiety negatively influences consumer confidence. The study emphasizes the need for balancing technological innovation with ethical data practices.

title: Job market signaling and inequality in the age of generative AI
affiliations: Bielefeld University - Center for Mathematical Economics and Leibniz Universität Hannover - Faculty of Economics and Management

detail.title: Job market signaling and inequality in the age of generative AI
detail.abstract: We introduce technological change into a Spence-type job market signaling model. Privately informed workers can signal their type to firms by acquiring an observable level of education, with higher-productivity workers facing lower marginal costs of education. In line with recent empirical evidence on the effects of generative artificial intelligence (AI), we assume that a higher level of AI widens the productivity gap between high and medium types, while narrowing the gap between medium and low types. We first show that there is a unique equilibrium that satisfies the D1 criterion. Second, in our main result, we show that increasing the level of AI increases the education level of high types but decreases that of medium types. Thus, AI increases education inequality between high-productivity types and the other groups.

title: The Green-Trust Framework: Evaluating the Synergy of AI and Blockchain in Enhancing Consumer Trust for Sustainability Marketing.

detail.title: The Green-Trust Framework: Evaluating the Synergy of AI and Blockchain in Enhancing Consumer Trust for Sustainability Marketing.
detail.abstract: In today's rapidly evolving market, sustainability has become a critical factor influencing consumer purchasing decisions. Consumers demand transparency and ethical behavior from brands, yet greenwashing and misleading claims continue to undermine trust. Emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain offer unique solutions to enhance consumer confidence in sustainable practices. This paper introduces the Green-Trust Framework, a conceptual model that combines AI and Blockchain to strengthen consumer trust in sustainability marketing. The framework leverages AI for data analysis, verification of claims, and personalized communication, while Blockchain provides transparency and immutability in supply chains. Through conceptual exploration and real-world application scenarios, this research highlights how the synergy of these technologies can build a trustworthy, ethical, and consumer-centric sustainability ecosystem. Finally, the paper discusses the benefits, limitations, and future research directions to guide marketers, regulators, and organizations in adopting technology-driven trust mechanisms.

title: Impact of Covid-19 on Consumer Buying Behaviour: A Study Among Employed Consumers in Malappuram District

detail.title: Impact of Covid-19 on Consumer Buying Behaviour: A Study Among Employed Consumers in Malappuram District

detail.abstract: The global spread of COVID-19 created unprecedented disruptions in economic activities and daily life, leading to significant changes in consumer purchasing behaviour. This study examines how the pandemic influenced the buying behaviour of consumers, with special reference to employed individuals in Malappuram district. The research aims to identify the major factors that affected purchasing decisions during the pandemic, analyze the changes in consumption patterns of household goods compared to the period before the pandemic, and understand the difficulties experienced by consumers while purchasing essential items.The study is descriptive in nature and is based on both primary and secondary sources of data. Primary data were collected from 160 respondents through a structured questionnaire using convenience sampling. Various statistical tools such as mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and non-parametric tests were used to analyze the collected data.The results indicate that the pandemic significantly influenced consumer priorities and purchasing behaviour. Consumers increased their spending on essential and hygiene-related products while reducing purchases of non-essential goods. Lockdown restrictions, health concerns, supply shortages, and income uncertainty were found to be major factors affecting consumer decisions. The study highlights that crisis situations such as pandemics can reshape consumption patterns and accelerate shifts toward safer and more necessity-driven purchasing behaviour.

title: Labor Risk and the Implied Cost of Equity Capital: Evidence from Firms' Exposure to Opioid Abuse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest related to this research.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of an important public health emergency on corporate financing costs. We document that firms' higher exposure to opioid abuse is associated with a higher implied cost of equity capital. Relying on the staggered adoption of state-level Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs, which exogenously reduce firms' exposure to opioid abuse, we establish causality. The adverse effects of opioid exposure are exacerbated for firms with low bargaining power relative to their employees, specifically, for firms that are more labor intensive and for those facing more stringent labor protection laws. Moreover, these effects exist for firms relying on high-skilled labor as well as those relying on low-skilled labor. We rule out demand-side risk from opioid-exposed customers as an alternative explanation. Overall, our evidence shows that equity investors can identify labor risk arising from public health emergencies and demand compensation for bearing this risk.

title: Crisis, Policy, and Technology: How External Shocks Reallocate Scholarly Attention in Innovation Research
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Crisis, Policy, and Technology: How External Shocks Reallocate Scholarly Attention in Innovation Research
detail.abstract: External shocks can redirect scholarly attention, but little is known about how different types of shocks reshape research agendas across countries. This paper studies how three shocks — the Industrie 4.0 policy initiative (2011), the COVID-19 pandemic (2020), and the public release of ChatGPT (2022) — reallocated direct scholarly attention in innovation research. We analyze 6,162 country-focused innovation studies on South Korea, Japan, Germany, and the United States published between 2000 and 2025, classifying each paper’s direct engagement with each shock using a validated text-based measure.The three shocks produce markedly different attention signatures. COVID-19 generates the fastest and broadest response, appearing across multiple countries within one half-year. By contrast, ChatGPT produces only sparse early signals and enters the published literature more slowly than COVID-19; received-date evidence suggests that this slower appearance reflects researcher response time rather than editorial processing. Industrie 4.0 displays a strikingly different pattern: it appears only after a five-year delay and is heavily concentrated in Germany-focused research. Using a difference-in-differences design, we obtain directional evidence that Germany-focused research exhibits roughly a 1 percentage point higher post-announcement I4.0 attention share, consistent with origin-country amplification. Qualitative thematic coding further shows that German I4.0 research is broadly diagnostic rather than celebratory, focusing on adoption barriers, competency gaps, and related implementation challenges.Together, these findings suggest that scholarly attention is not a neutral reflection of real-world need. Policy-origin shocks and crisis shocks restructure research agendas through different channels and on different timescales, and conceptual ownership of a policy label can diverge from implementation leadership.​

detail.abstract:
Purpose: The More Productive Brazil (BMP) program is a public policy aimed at improving the productivity of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. A novel element of the BMP has been the professional training of employees in Lean manufacturing techniques. This study analyzes the extension of gaps between workers' skills and employer demands, details the BMP's approach, and analyzes whether it leads to successful mitigation using the food manufacturing sector as a case study.

 Approach: Primary data is collected through online questionnaires from managers and participant employees. The empirical strategy follows an evaluation approach, examining whether reported changes in skills and operational performance are consistent with the program's intended mechanisms. Descriptive statistical analysis is used to evaluate the consistency between program design and reported outcomes. 

Findings: The responses indicate that technical skill deficits are the most prominent component of existing skill gaps, compounded by firms' limited resources to support worker training. Respondents broadly acknowledge the negative consequences of these gaps in four dimensions-material waste, errors and rework, delays in production, and low productivity. There is strong agreement that the professional training provided by the BMP caused higher interest in firm productivity, acquisition of new skills, and improved performance along these dimensions.

 Originality: The study contributes new evidence on how workforce-oriented training policies can address productivity constraints in small and medium-sized firms within developing economies. By linking firms' perceived skill gaps to behavioral and performance-related outcomes, it provides insights into mechanisms through which Leanbased training can translate into operational improvements.

title: Unequal Burden of Growth: Housing Cost Pressures on Renters Near High-Profile Firm Entries
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia Institute of Technology

keywords: Firm Entry and Local Economic Shocks

detail.abstract: Attracting high-profile firms is a central place-based development strategy used by state and local governments to boost employment, capital investment, and long-term growth. While the economic spillovers of such firm entries are well documented, their unintended effects on housing markets remain underexplored. This study examines how the arrival of high-profile firms affects rental housing affordability in Georgia communities officially recognized by the state's economic development agency. Using original firm-level data and a near-decade panel of census tract-level affordability outcomes from 2013-2021, we employ staggered difference-indifferences designs to estimate the causal impacts of firm entries on renter cost burdens across income groups. Results show that these entries significantly increase cost burdens among moderate-income renters earning 80-120 percent of the area median income, while effects are muted or negligible for lower-and higher-income renters. The findings challenge conventional wisdom and prevailing narratives that lower-income households are most vulnerable to housing market disruptions; instead, the most pronounced affordability pressures arise among moderate-income renters who often fall outside eligibility for traditional housing assistance. The implications reveal a critical blind spot in both housing policy and economic development discourse, suggesting the need for proactive affordable housing strategies to mitigate uneven consequences of firm-led growth.

detail.abstract: This study examines the evolution of reciprocal tariff uncertainty and its short-run impact on the Indian textile sector during key phases of trade policy signalling under the Trump administration. A mediabased Reciprocal Tariff Sentiment Index is constructed to capture the tone and intensity of tariff-related discussions from September 2024 to September 2025. To assess financial market responses during various phases of uncertainty, the study employs an event-study framework using daily stock price data for major Indian textile firms, with over 40 per cent of sectoral market capitalisation and significant presence in the US market. The results show heterogeneous market reactions across policy events. While the "America First" memorandum in January 2025 generated significantly negative abnormal returns, subsequent announcements that reduced relative uncertainty-particularly the April 2, 2025, Liberation Day tariff clarification-elicited positive market responses. In contrast, later announcements involving higher tariff rates and penalties led to renewed negative reactions, reflecting heightened concerns about trade disruptions. Furthermore, that a one-standard-deviation increase in the U.S. Trade Policy Uncertainty (TPU) index contemporaneously reduces month-over-month textile export growth by approximately 0.1 percentage points, consistent with documented uncertainty aversion in export decisions. Our findings highlight that long-run effects remain ambiguous, reflecting offsetting firmlevel adaptation, supply chain reorientation, and evolving policy expectations; however, our evidence underscores the critical macroeconomic stabilization benefit of transparent, timely trade policy communication. 1 Richa Saini Rawat and Shreya Gupta are both Managers from Monetary Policy Department. detail.title: IASCA: The International AI Safety Certification Authority — A Framework for Independent AI Governance
detail.abstract: This proposal introduces the International AI Safety Certification Authority (IASCA), an independent, internationally governed body for mandatory pre-deployment safety certification of frontier AI models. Modelled after the IAEA, FAA, and FDA, IASCA employs a zero-knowledge testing architecture that evaluates model safety through behavioural probing without accessing proprietary weights, training data, or architecture. The framework addresses the demonstrated failure of industry self-regulation, proposes a treaty-based governance structure with anti-capture provisions, and outlines a phased implementation roadmap from voluntary pilot to mandatory certification within five years. The economic model follows the FDA's PDUFA precedent, with progressive certification fees representing 0.1-1% of model training costs.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces three new socioeconomic terms-Parasitocracy, Parasitocratic, and Parasitonomics-as structural descriptors within governance science. These terms are not ideological labels, nor moral judgments. They are analytical instruments developed to evaluate whether governance systems are structurally constrained to serve the public or structurally aligned to serve power. 
The paper proposes a Democracy-Parasitocracy spectrum and argues that governance drift toward power-serving alignment is predictable when authority is insufficiently constrained by enforceable responsibility. The objective is to establish a neutral diagnostic vocabulary capable of supporting future empirical measurement and comparative analysis.

This framework does not classify specific countries or regimes. It introduces analytical terminology for governance assessment.

This paper contributes to governance science by introducing a structural vocabulary for evaluating public-serving versus power-serving institutional alignment.
