detail.abstract:
Most of us remember learning about natural selection back in school and have a sense of some of its everyday implications, like the risks of overusing antibiotics. Yet there are still many things that most of us fail to appreciate about evolution--including just how useful it can be to understand. Force of Nature explores how we misunderstand and neglect natural selection to our detriment, both missing opportunities to better achieve our goals and, sometimes, even imperiling lives. 

Through vivid and surprising examples ranging from medicine, psychology, and AI to economics, engineering, and beyond, we see how a finer grasp of natural selection can help open new horizons in cancer treatment and space exploration; create faster machines and better robots; design more effective, just laws; and more.  Force of Nature shows how, properly understood, evolution may be even more powerful than we may think.   [This SSRN document provides the Introduction of the book, excerpted with permission.]

title: CLIMATE POLICY IN A MEAN FIELD GAME OF HETEROGENEOUS COUNTRIES
affiliations: Banque Centrale du Luxembourg and Banque Centrale du Luxembourg

detail.title: CLIMATE POLICY IN A MEAN FIELD GAME OF HETEROGENEOUS COUNTRIES
detail.abstract: Recent empirical evidence reveals an income gradient in support for climate action: individuals in wealthier countries are less willing to pay than those in poorer ones. What explains this gradient, and what does it imply for international cooperation? We answer these questions by developing an integrated assessment model with a continuum of countries, formulated as a mean field game characterized by two partial differential equations and two ordinary differential equations. We calibrate the model usingeconomic and climate data and show that it reproduces key past evolutions. We then quantify the impacts of the introduction of a carbon tax on individual countries. Poorer countries, facing higher marginal utility of consumption, cut consumption less to cushion the decline in capital accumulation caused by climate damages. As a result, they suffer larger relative losses from climate change and gain more from mitigation, making them more inclined to accept a global carbon tax. This gradient has stark implications for cooperation: even when a carbon tax large enough to contain temperature increases benefits most countries, the richest might oppose. Redistributing global carbon tax proceeds uniformly across countries or recycling them as green investment subsidies need not overcome this reluctance.

title: Blocking the Blockers?
affiliations: Banco de España

detail.title: Blocking the Blockers?
detail.abstract: I study how firms’ defensive investments affect aggregate total factor productivity (TFP) in a general-equilibrium model where incumbents invest both to raise productivity and to deter entry or imitation; entry occurs either by new firms into existing markets or as a leading firm in an entirely new product line. Calibrated to U.S. data to match the joint relationships between intangible investment intensity, firm productivity, market share, and firm size, the model shows that cracking down on defensive investments increases aggregate TFP by 4 percent, driven primarily by higher technical efficiency resulting from improved firm-level productivity. This gain is partially offset by a reduction in product variety; absent this effect, the TFP increase would be twice as large. Profit taxes targeted at single-product leaders—those most prone to block imitation—combined with selective subsidies for entrants introducing new products can strengthen firm-level productivity while limiting losses in product variety. Firm-level evidence from U.S. data supports these mechanisms.

title: Automation, Income Distribution, and Aggregate Demand in a Two-Asset HANK Model
affiliations: Chonnam National University

detail.title: Automation, Income Distribution, and Aggregate Demand in a Two-Asset HANK Model
detail.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence and robotics are reshaping production, but how does this transformation affect workers and consumers when many households live paycheck to paycheck? We study this question in a macroeconomic model where firms choose how many tasks to automate and households differ in their access to savings. We find that automation lowers wages and the share of income going to workers, reducing spending by households who cannot easily save. During the transition, employment initially booms due to investment but then declines persistently. Monetary policy becomes more powerful in highly automated economies, but cannot fully offset the demand shortfall. These findings suggest that automation policies should combine monetary accommodation with fiscal redistribution to sustain broad-based demand.

title: The Simulacrum of Intelligence
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Simulacrum of Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Four years after ChatGPT's November 2022 launch inaugurated the mainstream "AI era," this paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) constitute genuine intelligence or a convincing simulacrum thereof. Drawing on 40+ sources across computer science, cognitive science, and philosophy of mind, the paper synthesizes seven independent technical lines of evidence — including the stochastic parrot critique (Bender et al., 2021), formal proofs of hallucination inevitability (Xu et al., 2024; Kalai & Vempala, 2024), the fragility of LLM reasoning under trivial perturbation (Mirzadeh et al., 2025), benchmark contamination, absent world models, scaling diminishing returns, and the symbol grounding problem — with four philosophical frameworks: the Chinese Room argument updated for self-learning systems, Floridi's theory of agency without intelligence, the consciousness gap as assessed under Integrated Information Theory and Global Workspace Theory, and Baudrillard's simulacra as applied to machine-generated signs of cognition. 

The analysis finds that these independent dimensions converge on a single conclusion: current LLMs produce statistically sophisticated outputs that mimic the form of intelligence without instantiating its substance. Contemporary deployment evidence (2024–2026) reinforces this finding, with 95% of organizations reporting zero return on generative AI investments, hallucinated legal citations exceeding 700 documented cases, and the scaling hypothesis encountering diminishing returns acknowledged by its own architects. The paper engages the strongest counterarguments — including emergent internal representations, grounding through distributional semantics, and the systems reply to the Chinese Room — and finds them insufficient to bridge the gap between simulation and understanding. 

It concludes by recovering J.C.R. Licklider's (1960) vision of human-computer symbiosis, arguing that the most productive path forward lies not in pursuing artificial general intelligence through current architectures but in the complementary partnership between human judgment and machine computation that the field's founding visionary originally proposed.

title: Cash Crops, Settlement Patterns, and Indigenous Population Growth: The Role of Wine in Colonial Algeria (1900–1950)
affiliations: Universidad de Alcalá, Universitat Barcelona and Charles III University of Madrid

detail.title: Cash Crops, Settlement Patterns, and Indigenous Population Growth: The Role of Wine in Colonial Algeria (1900–1950)
detail.abstract: This paper examines how export-oriented settler agriculture shaped the spatial distribution of indigenous populations in colonial Algeria. By the early twentieth century, Algeria had become one of the world’s largest wine producers and the principal supplier of wine to metropolitan France. We construct a commune-level panel dataset combining census measures of the indigenous population with indicators of viticultural intensity derived from agricultural reports. Exploiting variation in early exposure to viticulture across communes, we show that indigenous population growth became increasingly concentrated in high-viticulture areas from the late 1920s onward, with divergence intensifying during the Great Depression. This pattern is consistent with in-migration driven by the relatively continuous labor demand of viticulture—unlike more seasonal crops—followed by reduced outward mobility as alternative employment opportunities contracted. These findings indicate persistent spatial differences in population growth across communes. This study provides systematic quantitative evidence linking the labor demands of settler monoculture to the spatial concentration of indigenous populations in colonial Algeria.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Regulatory Sandboxes: Models, Evolution and Strategic Implications in EU, USA and China
affiliations: University San Raffaele Roma and European University of Rome

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of Regulatory Sandboxes: Models, Evolution and Strategic Implications in EU, USA and China
detail.abstract: The article compares the design, evolution, and strategic uses of regulatory sandboxes across the European Union, the United States, and the People’s Republic of China. Using a comparative lens to conduct an analysis of law and politics, the authors demonstrate that sandboxes are not neutral test beds but rather jurisdiction-specific governance instruments that strike a balance between innovation, legality, risk, and market structure. The European Union trajectory shifts from soft-law facilitators to hard-law experimentation, most visibly evident in the DLT Pilot Regime and the AI Act’s mandatory sandboxes, which embed proportionality, rights, and supervisory convergence while exposing the “sandbox paradox” of potential competitive distortions. The United States landscape is presented as decentralized, with dynamic state programs coexisting with cautious federal soft law, yielding agility but weak interoperability and uneven consumer protection. The People’s Republic of China model is analyzed as centrally steered, soft-law heavy, and incumbent-oriented, aligning pilots with industrial policy, financial stability and technological sovereignty, yet marked by opacity and limited open access. Sandboxes thus appear as transitional constitutional technologies: effective when disciplined by legality, accountability and competitive neutrality, and when used to inform, not replace, enduring regulatory reform.

title: Institutional Field Dynamics: A Force Field Model of Multi-Actor Governance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Institutional Field Dynamics: A Force Field Model of Multi-Actor Governance
detail.abstract: Institutional theory describes mechanisms of isomorphism, inertia, and path dependence, but these accounts remain largely qualitative and do not generate quantitative predictions about which institutional configurations produce which dynamics. This paper formalizes institutional dynamics as a force field system in which actors move through an institutional configuration space under three types of force: intrinsic motivation toward individual ideals, social influence mediated by an asymmetric power matrix, and institutional pressure imposed by policy architecture. Policy is modeled not as direct instruction but as transformation of the field itself. The model generates diagnostic metrics-coherence, friction, and power asymmetry-that characterize the structural health of an institutional configuration. Extensions include relational utility functions that make cooperation and conflict endogenous, dynamic evolution of the power matrix through interaction, and explicit attractor analysis that tests whether policy genuinely transforms the institutional landscape or merely shifts positions within it. A demonstration case-Dutch tailored education reform (Passend Onderwijs, 2014)-shows that the model identifies structural failure modes that qualitative analysis alone does not predict: the reform produced multiple competing attractors under the actual policy configuration, with teacher outcomes spanning the entire configuration space depending on initial conditions, versus structurally convergent outcomes under an alternative configuration with symmetric influence and compatible incentives. Robustness analysis confirms that multi-stability persists across ±50% parameter perturbation and six alternative expert configurations. The model identifies structural multi-stability as a computable property of institutional configurations, enabling ex ante diagnosis of policy fragility. The framework applies as a computational diagnostic layer on top of existing institutional theory to any multi-actor governance context where mandated actors engage with committed institutional architectures, including advisory governance, regulatory design, and participatory democracy.

title: Stablecoins and the Global Dollar System
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco

detail.title: Stablecoins and the Global Dollar System
detail.abstract: The dollar has served for almost a century as the dominant global currency for trade, settlement, and reserve purposes, creating immense benefits for the United States.  Amid recent concerns that the dollar’s grip may be weakening, key policymakers view the emergence of dollar-pegged stablecoins—cryptocurrencies that promise to maintain a value of $1 per token—as a tool to help entrench the dollar’s hegemonic status.  Continued dollar dominance may benefit the United States, but wide uptake of stablecoins could significantly undermine U.S. policy interests along two other dimensions: maintaining financial stability and leveraging the global payment system for law enforcement and foreign policy purposes.  Congress recently attempted to provide regulatory clarity for stablecoins in order to bolster dollar hegemony while addressing these risks with the passage of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act) in the summer of 2025.  This Essay argues that the Act falls short of addressing the risks, explores the implications of these shortcomings, and considers possible policy responses.

title: The Adaptive Signaling Economy
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Adaptive Signaling Economy
detail.abstract:
LStandard economic theory models individuals as rational agents maximizing utility under constraints. While behavioral economics has introduced psychological deviations from rationality, it still largely abstracts from the evolutionary origins of economic behavior.

This paper proposes a unifying framework, The Adaptive Signaling Economy (ASE), grounded in ethology and evolutionary biology. We argue that a substantial share of human economic behavior is best understood as adaptive signaling, inherited from animal social systems, where economic actions primarily function to signal status, fitness, trustworthiness, and group membership rather than to maximize material payoff alone.

By integrating animal signaling theory, evolutionary stable strategies, and economic choice, we formalize a model in which markets operate as signaling arenas. The framework explains persistent economic anomalies such as conspicuous consumption, unpaid labor, excessive competition, speculative behavior, and reputation-driven markets. The theory generates testable predictions that diverge from both neoclassical and standard behavioral models, offering a biologically grounded foundation for economic analysis.

title: A Behavioral Analysis of Dual-Interpreted News Events
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Behavioral Analysis of Dual-Interpreted News Events
detail.abstract:
This research paper delves into the dual-interpretation nature of some news events-moments where headlines trigger conflicting market signals – and how this market condition drives price discovery. EMH (Fama, 1970) Suggests that information is ‘priced in’ instantly. However, real-world markets are rarely that clear. By Analyzing over thousands news events and categorizing them based on market participants’ reaction and behavior, I have mentioned few news headlines that carries ambiguous, multi-layered narrative. I will use one news event covering the Recessionary pivot narrative after the August 4th 2024 Nonfarm payroll release.

My findings suggest that purely quantitative models often fail during these regime shifts because they lack situational awareness. To solve this, I propose a "Dynamic Execution" framework—a hybrid approach that blends context-heavy programming with discretionary human oversight.  Ultimately, the data shows that in today’s markets, the context surrounding a headline is just as vital for valuation as the news itself.

title: Reality Salience: Neurocognitive Prioritization of Information in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Reality Salience: Neurocognitive Prioritization of Information in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Human cognition depends on the ability to distinguish external reality from imagination, inference, or fabrication. While narratives can influence beliefs regardless of factual status, the mechanisms by which the brain assigns differential priority to reality-relevant information remain under-theorized. This paper introduces the concept of reality salience, defined as the degree to which information is processed as consequential for real-world action and therefore receives enhanced weighting within attentional, mnemonic, and decision-making systems.

Integrating research on reality and source monitoring, narrative transportation, epistemic vigilance, dual-process cognition, and neuroimaging of factual versus fictional processing, the paper proposes a three-stage neurocognitive model comprising source inference, authenticity evaluation, and priority allocation. The model explains how authenticity judgments modulate trust calibration, memory consolidation, and behavioral readiness.

The rise of AI-generated media introduces a novel epistemic condition in which traditional authenticity cues—such as fluency and coherence—are decoupled from the epistemic constraints and accountability structures that typically render them informative in human communication. This decoupling may miscalibrate evaluative processes, leading to over-acceptance of synthetic content or generalized distrust. The paper derives testable predictions regarding cognition in AI-saturated information environments and outlines implications for epistemic resilience.

detail.abstract: Recent macro-financial perturbations in the real global economy have unveiled strident differences in economies' capacity to maintain investment amidst market instability, stressing the increasing policy worth of financial resilience as a buffering anchor of actual market activity. This paper introduces a combined econometric exploration of financial resilience (AFRI) as a determining factor of domestic investment under both financial vulnerability (FVI) and commodity market volatility (CMPV) across 82 economies, covering the 2005-2024 period. This paper builds on the IMF's resilience framework (IMF, 2023), to develop and test four hypotheses about linear interaction, nonlinear, and distributional impacts of absorptive resilience.

title: Simulating Residential Growth in Fragmented Housing Markets: A Stepwise Model for Cape Town
affiliations: City of Cape Town, City of Cape Town, City of Cape Town and City of Cape Town

detail.title: Simulating Residential Growth in Fragmented Housing Markets: A Stepwise Model for Cape Town

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was commissioned by the City of Cape Town. The authors declare no other competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
