title: Fast Payment Systems and Deposit Dynamics: Evidence from Brazil's Pix
affiliations: FGV-EBAPE, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio) and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Brazilian School of Public and Business Administration (EBAPE)

detail.title: Fast Payment Systems and Deposit Dynamics: Evidence from Brazil's Pix
detail.abstract: Deposits are the foundation of bank funding and financial stability. We investigate how Brazil's instant payment system, Pix, reshapes deposit dynamics. Pix, launched by the Central Bank of Brazil in November 2020, enables real-time transfers 24/7 at minimal cost. Using monthly bank-municipality panel data from 2010-2025, we examine how Pix changes bank deposit levels and their volatility. We take advantage of three important features of Pix that facilitate identification. First, participation in Pix was mandatory for large banks, making the reform exogenous to bank characteristics and eliminating selection bias. Second, adoption and usage decisions were made by consumers and firms after launch, generating variation in Pix intensity across banks and municipalities. Third, the shift from traditional payment instruments to instant transfers was unanticipated, creating a quasi-natural experiment in deposit dynamics. First, we find that Pix significantly increases bank deposits, consistent with greater financial inclusion and faster money circulation. Second, Pix increases deposit volatility locally, reflecting faster reallocation of funds across institutions. Third, Pix reduces deposit volatility at the national bank level, suggesting banks benefit from geographic diversification of deposit flows. We validate these findings by analyzing a large temporary shock to public trust in Pix in January 2025 triggered by fake news regarding taxation. During that episode, deposit levels temporarily dropped and their volatility spiked. Overall, our study demonstrates that fast payment innovations significantly transform the way how banks attract and retain deposit funding.

title: Impact of Environmental Measures on International Trade (with focus on EU CBAM & WTO law)
affiliations: Maharaja Agrasen Institute of Management Studies

detail.title: Impact of Environmental Measures on International Trade (with focus on EU CBAM & WTO law)
detail.abstract:
The increasing integration of environmental concerns into international trade policy has given rise to complex legal challenges within the framework of the World Trade Organization (WTO). One such development is the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which seeks to address carbon leakage by imposing a carbon cost on certain imported goods. While the measure aims to promote climate objectives and ensure a level playing field between domestic and foreign producers, it raises significant questions regarding its compatibility with established WTO principles, particularly those of non-discrimination under the Most Favoured Nation and National Treatment obligations.

This paper examines the legal and policy implications of CBAM within the WTO framework, analysing whether it constitutes a legitimate environmental measure or a disguised restriction on international trade. It further explores the scope of justification under Article XX of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), with reference to relevant WTO jurisprudence. The study also considers the perspective of developing countries, particularly India, highlighting concerns relating to equity, compliance burdens, and trade competitiveness.

The paper argues that while CBAM may be justified in principle as an environmental measure, its legality ultimately depends on its design and implementation. A balanced and context-sensitive approach is necessary to reconcile trade liberalisation with climate objectives, ensuring that environmental measures do not undermine the foundational principles of fairness and non-discrimination in international trade law.

title: The Bifurcation Index (BFX): A Composite Indicator of Distributional Economic Divergence

detail.title: The Bifurcation Index (BFX): A Composite Indicator of Distributional Economic Divergence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Bifurcation Analytics and creator of the Bifurcation Index. The index is a proprietary product of Bifurcation Analytics. No external funding was received. All data are sourced from publicly available U.S. government repositories.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All data sources are free and publicly available via the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) API.

detail.abstract: The Bifurcation Index (BFX) is a proprietary composite economic indicator that quantifies the structural divergence between upper-income and lower-income economic realities in the United States. The index synthesizes 15 analytical components derived from 33 FRED data series across five equally-weighted pillars — Consumer Spending, Labor Market, Housing, Financial Assets, and Consumer Sentiment — into a single interpretable score from 0 to 100. A reading of 50 represents the pre-pandemic baseline established over the January 2008 – December 2019 reference period. All component series are stationary by design: ratios, YoY growth rates, bounded rates, or detrended via ratio to a 120-month trailing moving average. A single five-step pipeline applies a 3-month centered moving average followed by fixed-baseline z-scoring to convert each component to a 0–100 scale. Published BFX values are the direct equal-weighted average of the five pillar scores — final on the date of publication with no composite-level smoothing. At publication, the BFX reads 57 (Slightly Above Baseline), with pillar scores of: Consumer Spending 81, Labor Market 39, Housing 50, Financial Assets 55, Consumer Sentiment 61. Empirical validation on the constructed backtest demonstrates statistically significant leading relationships with consumer sector relative performance, credit card delinquency trends, sector return dispersion, and consumer sentiment — all in the expected direction. The 2008–2026 historical series is a constructed backtest; live publication commenced March 2026.

title: Entry, Allocation, and Welfare in Successive Oligopoly
affiliations: Lancaster University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Entry, Allocation, and Welfare in Successive Oligopoly
detail.abstract: We study a successive oligopoly with free entry at both stages of production and find two sources of inefficiency: a misallocation of firms across stages and an inefficient level of total entry.  The direction of misallocation depends on  the curvature of inverse demand for the final good. Whether entry is excessive or insufficient depends on how misallocation affects industry profit and on a business-stealing externality based on average industry output.

title: Exploring Macro-Constitutional Reality in Ukraine: Multi-Textual Insights from the Constitutional Court

detail.title: Exploring Macro-Constitutional Reality in Ukraine: Multi-Textual Insights from the Constitutional Court
detail.abstract: This chapter offers a deep and comprehensive analysis of Ukraine's constitutional framework by examining the applicability of the multi-textual constitution phenomenon to the national constitution. Although the 1996 Constitution of Ukraine is traditionally regarded as a single codified act, at least three additional documents can co-share some characteristics of the country's supreme law. These documents include, inter alia, (1) the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine, approved by a referendum on 1 December 1991, (2) the Law of Ukraine 'On Adoption of the Constitution of Ukraine and Its Entry into Force' adopted immediately after the Constitution, and (3) the Rules of Procedure of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, which, although technically a piece of ordinary legislation, has become a part of constitutional interpretation due to the Constitutional Court's activism. This research relies on normative analysis of relevant legal instruments and the case law of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine as key sources for understanding how the Constitution of Ukraine operates. The chapter demonstrates that the multi-textual constitution theory is not merely an intellectual construct but also possesses practical applicability, particularly in the case of Ukraine, where it contributes to the emergence of a 'macro-constitutional reality'.

title: Firm Hierarchies and Misallocation
affiliations: Duke University and Duke University

detail.title: Firm Hierarchies and Misallocation
detail.abstract: We study how internal hierarchies affect productivity, wages, and labor shares in Chinese manufacturing firms. Using detailed information on professional titles from the 2004 Annual Survey of Industrial Production, we construct firm-level measures of hierarchical structure and compare private firms with state-owned enterprises (SOEs). Private firms operate leaner hierarchies and exhibit rising labor productivity as organizational layers expand. In contrast, SOEs adopt prematurely deep and top-heavy hierarchies associated with declining labor productivity but higher wages. As a result, labor shares are substantially higher in SOEs. Counterfactual exercises show that distortions in hiring and organizational design account for a large fraction of the labor share gap between SOEs and private firms, pointing to inefficient internal organization as an important source of aggregate misallocation.

title: Research on Reliability Prediction of Fatigue Failure of Fast Mechanical Switch Insulation Rod Based on Voltage Quantization Characterization
affiliations: Anhui University, Anhui University, Anhui University, Anhui University and Anhui University

detail.title: Research on Reliability Prediction of Fatigue Failure of Fast Mechanical Switch Insulation Rod Based on Voltage Quantization Characterization
detail.abstract: This study addresses the challenges of accurately predicting the lifespan of insulation rods in fast mechanical switches under time-varying stress, including difficulties in on-site stress measurement and the lack of life dispersion characterization. We propose a fatigue reliability prediction method that combines direct voltage quantization with the inverse power law and Weibull distribution. To validate our COMSOL simulation model, we established a multi-voltage condition test platform. Using the damage equivalence principle, we extracted equivalent stress and developed a linear voltage-equivalent stress relationship. This led to the formulation of a direct voltage-life quantization equation through a dedicated inverse power law model. By integrating the Weibull distribution, we constructed a combined model that facilitates rapid life calculations without on-site stress testing. We introduced a progressive evaluation process that merges a deterministic loss account with a probabilistic reliability model. The model's generality was confirmed through tests under un-simulated working conditions, and it was applied to engineering tasks such as multi-condition life prediction, voltage fluctuation quantification, and extreme condition assessment. Results demonstrated that the combined model offers low prediction error and high efficiency, effectively quantifying allowable voltage fluctuation ranges. Safety assessments under extreme conditions were achieved via model extrapolation. This method effectively addresses the challenges of stress measurement and slow evaluation in on-site operations, offering an efficient and scalable solution for the reliable design and precise operation of insulation rods.

title: Regime-Aware Allocation for Robust Multi-Asset Portfolio Management
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Operations Research & Financial Engineering (ORFE) and

detail.title: Regime-Aware Allocation for Robust Multi-Asset Portfolio Management
detail.abstract: We develop a regime-based asset allocation framework for multi-asset portfolios that adapts exposures to evolving asset-level regimes, aiming to enhance long-term performance over passive benchmarks while limiting drawdowns and improving crisis resilience. The framework combines statistical jump models, which infer persistent latent bull and bear regimes from historical returns, with a supervised learning model that forecasts future regime transitions. Regime forecasts are integrated into standard allocation rules, including equal-weight and risk-parity, to demonstrate how regime awareness strengthens widely used strategies. Portfolio construction is further extended by testing gold as a fallback asset when all risky assets are bearish, reflecting its renewed appeal as a safe-haven amid recent market uncertainty. The framework is applied to U.S. equity, bond, and currency indices over the 1992-2025 period. Regime filters provide downside protection in equities, volatility reduction in bonds, and improved asymmetry in currencies, while their aggregation into portfolios yields higher Sharpe and Sortino ratios, smaller drawdowns, and resilience across major crises. Robustness checks confirm that these results are not dependent on auxiliary macro or sentiment features.

title: Rates Up, Balances Up: Uneven Monetary Transmission in Consumer Credit Markets
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Gies College of Business, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Gies College of Business, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Gies College of Business and UIUC

detail.title: Rates Up, Balances Up: Uneven Monetary Transmission in Consumer Credit Markets
detail.abstract: What happens to consumer borrowing when interest rates rise? Using a representative panel of consumer credit records and individual-level local projections, we show that contractionary monetary policy increases rather than reduces household debt. A 1 s.d. contractionary shock raises total debt by $3,967, or 7%, over three years. On the extensive margin, the number of credit accounts also increases in response to a contractionary shock. The effect is stronger and more persistent for financially constrained consumers. Mechanism evidence is consistent with an indirect channel: tighter policy weakens labor markets and household income, increasing reliance on credit among exposed borrowers. Our findings highlight an important distributional dimension of monetary transmission, as tightening raises indebtedness among vulnerable households.

title: Research on the Life Assessment of the Insulating Rod of a Fast Mechanical Switch Based on the Weibull Distribution and the Firefly Algorithm
affiliations: Department of Preventive Medicine, School of Health Sciences, Wuhan University, Anhui University and Anhui University

detail.title: Research on the Life Assessment of the Insulating Rod of a Fast Mechanical Switch Based on the Weibull Distribution and the Firefly Algorithm
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of increasingly stringent reliability requirements for fast mechanical switches in power systems, the life assessment of the insulating rod, a core component of fast mechanical switches, faces the challenges of insufficient credibility in pure simulation, high costs in pure testing, and limited coverage of operating conditions. To address this, this study proposes a method for predicting the life of insulating rods based on the three-parameter Weibull distribution and the firefly optimization algorithm, enabling reliable assessment of the rod life under multiple driving voltage conditions. First, a multi-physical coupling finite element model of the switch is established, and the validity of the model is verified through actual stress tests. Second, the failure life is calculated by combining the stress-life curve and the linear cumulative damage theory. Subsequently, the three-parameter Weibull distribution is used to fit the data, the parameters are globally optimized via the firefly algorithm, and the statistical characteristic indicators are derived in combination with the gamma function. The experimental verification and simulation expansion methods adopted in this study avoid the drawbacks of pure testing and pure simulation, providing a theoretical and engineering foundation for the reliability design and life assessment of key components of high-end equipment.

title: From Prenatal Fantasy to Collective Life: The Relational Architecture of Existence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Prenatal Fantasy to Collective Life: The Relational Architecture of Existence
detail.abstract: The beginning of human life shows that existence appears as an event of relationship. Even before conception occurs, the future child is often already situated within a field of desire, fantasy, and expectation belonging to others. Human existence emerges within a symbolic space where others have already thought of it or desired it. The birth of the human being therefore begins within a network of relationships, within which existence gradually acquires form. Biological Conception as a Primary Relational Event Biological conception itself already constitutes a relational event. Human life arises from the union of two cells that combine to create a new organism. From that moment onward, the organism itself is formed through cooperative processes among cells that differentiate, communicate, and coordinate in order to create tissues and organs. The heart, the brain, and all the systems of the body are products of this organized cellular articulation. Life, from its most elementary biological level to its most complex form of organization, emerges through processes of connection and cooperation.

title: Age-Sets and Gadaa-grades

detail.title: Age-Sets and Gadaa-grades
detail.abstract: This chapter examines the structural foundations of the Gadaa System by distinguishing and interrelating age-sets and Gadaa-grades as two core yet analytically distinct institutions. It explains that age-sets are universal eight-year biological cohorts organising the Oromo life cycle into developmental, mature, and retirement phases, while Gadaa-grades are genealogical-generation–based political stages through which members of a Gadaa party progress toward leadership (Luba) and subsequently retire through descending grades. The chapter clarifies that although the two systems ideally align for “right-born” sons—those born during the father’s designated dhaloota period—they are structurally independent, and misalignment is common. It further elaborates the forty-year generational separation between fathers and sons, the five-party succession system, and the principle of staggered power transfer, demonstrating how ritual timing, passage rites, military training, property rights, leadership formation, and civic responsibilities are integrated into a coherent socio-political order. By separating biological age from political progression, the chapter resolves terminological confusion and presents the Gadaa System as a complex, adaptive institution grounded in cyclical time, generational balance, and structured civic development.

title: Pyramidal Coherence: A Multi-Resolution Hidden Markov Framework for Regime-Multiplexed Strategy Selection in Equity Index Futures

detail.title: Pyramidal Coherence: A Multi-Resolution Hidden Markov Framework for Regime-Multiplexed Strategy Selection in Equity Index Futures

detail.abstract: We present a novel regime classification framework based on pyramidal coherence-the real-time measurement of agreement between Hidden Markov Models operating simultaneously at three temporal resolutions (5-minute, 15-minute, and 60-minute). Rather than attempting to predict future market states, we detect the structural integrity of the current regime by monitoring cross-resolution coherence dynamics. Our central finding is counter-intuitive: periods of coherence breakdown do not signal danger, but instead identify a distinct market microstructure-a high-entropy, mean-reverting environment-that is systematically exploitable. We formalize this as a regime multiplexer that routes capital to the strategy class best suited to the prevailing market character. A subsequent decomposition reveals that the type of coherence failure matters: divergence-driven instability produces tradeable mean-reversion, while acceleration-driven instability is adversarial-a distinction we term the poison sub-regime. We further extend the framework with a meta-allocation controller that monitors macro stress via drawdown depth and dynamically switches between concentrated and expanded portfolios. The two-layer adaptive system achieves a Sharpe ratio of 4.29, a Calmar ratio of 4.13, and annual P&L of $1,895 over 5.5 years of strictly walk-forward out-of-sample data, with every calendar year profitable. The meta-controller captures 82% more annual P&L than the concentrated portfolio while maintaining an identical maximum drawdown of $459.

title: The Resizing of America: How GLP-1s are Transitioning the Economy from Glut to Gap
affiliations: University of Connecticut

detail.title: The Resizing of America: How GLP-1s are Transitioning the Economy from Glut to Gap

detail.abstract: The widespread adoption of GLP-1s presents the country with a profound macroeconomic and cultural transition, shifting the nation from a decades-long "Glut" economy, defined by hyper-consumption, to an emerging "Gap" economy defined by intentional deficit. This paper examines the multi-sector disruption caused by the unnatural silencing of appetite and reward-seeking behaviors. Biologically, the rapid loss of lean muscle mass is creating a crisis of sarcopenic obesity. This forces the fitness and food industries to pivot from caloric deficit models to structural preservation and nutrient density. Psychologically, the blunting of mesolimbic dopamine transmission is triggering a collapse of addictive habits such as alcohol consumption, which results in voids in the ways in which some cope with stress. Industrially, this biological reset is fundamentally reallocating consumer capital. As grocery stores face severe contractions, industries such as apparel are experiencing a massive "resizing dividend." Ultimately, this research argues that while GLP-1s represent a triumph of modern metabolic pharmacology, the resulting "Gap" economy threatens to establish a new biological class divide, where the thin, toned body becomes the ultimate symbol of status.

title: Drill or Drop: Regulatory Enforcement under Section 94 of the Petroleum Industry Act and the Future of Nigeria's Upstream Petroleum Sector.
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Drill or Drop: Regulatory Enforcement under Section 94 of the Petroleum Industry Act and the Future of Nigeria's Upstream Petroleum Sector.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The work is entirely my brain child.

detail.abstract: The renewed enforcement of the "drill or drop" principle by the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) represents one of the most consequential regulatory developments in Nigeria's upstream petroleum sector since the enactment of the Petroleum Industry Act 2021. Founded in Section 94 of the Act, the rule requires licence holders to actively develop hydrocarbon discoveries within a definite period or relinquish the asset. This article examines the legal foundation of the drill or drop rule, the policy prospects behind its renewed enforcement, and the broader implications for Nigeria's upstream petroleum industry. It argues that the policy represents a deliberate shift from a system in which petroleum licences were often retained without development towards a more performance-based regulatory regime. While the rule has the potential to unlock dormant assets and improve resource utilisation, its effectiveness will depend on regulatory consistency, investment conditions and the financial capacity of industry participants.

title: Carbon Taxes and ESG Compensation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Carbon Taxes and ESG Compensation
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how ESG-linked executive compensation interacts with carbon taxation in a multitask principal-agent framework. A risk-neutral principal with financial and environmental preferences incentivizes a risk-averse manager to exert productive and abatement effort while facing an exogenous carbon tax on emissions. We show that, in the absence of ESG incentives, carbon taxes reduce emissions mainly by lowering production. In contrast, ESG-linked compensation shifts emission reductions toward increased abatement, allowing the principal to raise expected payoff while simultaneously reducing emissions, both with and without carbon taxation. However, carbon taxes narrow the range of feasible ESG preferences and, at high levels, may induce excessive abatement, potentially leading to negative net emissions. Our results highlight the importance of aligning internal incentive design with external climate regulation. The interplay of ESG compensation and carbon taxes should also be considered from a regulatory perspective.

title: What Makes New Work Different from More Work?
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Utrecht University and

detail.title: What Makes New Work Different from More Work?
detail.abstract: We study the role of expertise in new work - novel occupational roles that emerge as technological and economic conditions evolve - using newly available 1940 and 1950 Census Complete Count files and confidential American Community Survey data from 2011-2023. We show that new work is systematically distinct from simply more work in existing occupations in four respects. First, it attracts workers with distinct characteristics: new work is disproportionately performed by younger and more educated workers, even within detailed occupation-industry cells. Second, new work commands economically significant wage premiums that persist beyond workers' initial entry into new work, consistent with returns to scarce, specialized expertise rather than temporary market disequilibrium. Third, these premiums decline across vintages as expertise diffuses, with `newer' new work commanding larger premiums than older new work. Fourth, the emergence of new work can be traced to specific demand shocks in particular locations and time periods, suggesting that expertise formation responds systematically to economic opportunities. These findings suggest that new work serves as a countervailing force to automation-driven job displacement not merely by creating additional employment, but also by generating new domains of human expertise that command market premiums. This expertise-based mechanism helps explain both the expanding variety of work activities across decades and the historical resilience of the labor share.

title: Russian Crime Victimization Survey: Pooled Cross-Sections and a Longitudinal Panel, 2018–2024
affiliations: European University at St. Petersburg (EUSP), The Institute for the Rule of Law, European University at St. Petersburg, ,  and European University at St. Petersburg

detail.title: Russian Crime Victimization Survey: Pooled Cross-Sections and a Longitudinal Panel, 2018–2024
detail.abstract: Victimization surveys are a valuable alternative source of information on crime, allowing for the study of incidents unreported to the police. We present the Russian Crime Victimization Survey (RCVS): harmonized pooled data from three nationally representative cross-sections (2018, 2021, 2024) and a longitudinal component (2021–2024). The RCVS is the only repeated nationwide victimization survey in Russia. Each wave employs random digit dialing and a screening design that interviews both victims and non-victims until 3,000 victim interviews are reached. Across three waves, 42,572 respondents were interviewed, with 3,456 re-interviewed as a part of the longitudinal sample. The data capture the "dark figure of crime" missed by official statistics and support research on trust in the police, reporting behavior, the fear of crime, cybercrime, and victimization dynamics.

title: AI, Output, and Employment
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin and

detail.title: AI, Output, and Employment
detail.abstract: Does artificial intelligence (AI) increase productivity - and does it displace workers? We examine aggregate effects using administrative data covering essentially all U.S. employers in a difference-in-differences design exploiting occupational AI exposure across industries and states. A one standard deviation increase in exposure raises output by 7%, with effects emerging in 2021 when enterprise AI tools entered the market. Employment effects follow the same timing but diverge by exposure type: where AI likely requires human collaboration, employment rises 4%; where AI can perform tasks independently, we find no significant employment effect. Results are robust to state-by-year and industry-by-year fixed effects and suggest AI has caused a decrease in the labor share of income.

title: Market Inefficiency in Digital Asset Markets: Cross-Market Dynamics, Determinants, and Policy Implications
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Market Inefficiency in Digital Asset Markets: Cross-Market Dynamics, Determinants, and Policy Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of fragmented arbitrage with heterogeneous settlement frictions and derives five propositions, which are evaluated across spot, derivatives, and stablecoin markets using a multi-source panel from April 2019 to January 2026. Capital-constrained arbitrageurs face a shared wealth constraint that generates cross-channel amplification when frictions tighten. The dislocations are large: average Bitcoin cross-exchange dispersion is 11 basis points (exceeding 587 basis points during stress), annualized perpetual funding-implied carry averages 12.5% with substantial time variation, and stablecoin peg deviations spike during banking and liquidity stress. In repeated-outcome panel projections with date-clustered inference, realized volatility is robustly associated with daily dispersion, while bid-ask spread coefficients are positive but imprecise. Cross-exchange dispersion was about 68% lower in the post-ETF period (2024–2026) than in the pre-ETF period (2019–2023), consistent with a secular trend toward improved market integration, though the simple pre/post comparison around the approval date shows only a marginally insignificant decrease (−0.64 basis points, p = 0.095). Stress episodes produce sharp but transient spikes. Rolling-window VAR connectedness analysis reveals that stress transmission increases from 11.7% to 17.3% across inefficiency channels. A composite Market Inefficiency Index detects four of six major stress episodes at the 2σ threshold, with the May 2021 leverage unwind producing the largest dislocation (9.6σ). The results are more consistent with transparency-based and integration-enhancing regulation than with fragmentation-inducing restrictions.

title: Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the US
affiliations: , Vanderbilt University, Academic Dean, Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS),  and WZB Berlin Social Science Center

detail.title: Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the US
detail.abstract: This paper combines international evidence from worker and firm surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026 to document large gaps in AI adoption, both between the US and Europe and across European countries. Cross-country differences in worker demographics and firm composition account for an important share of these gaps. AI adoption, within and across countries, is also closely linked to firm personnel management practices and whether firms actively encourage AI use by workers. Micro-level evidence suggests that AI generates meaningful time savings for many workers. At the macro level, in recent years industries with higher AI adoption rates have experienced faster productivity growth. While we do not establish causality, this relationship is statistically significant and similar in magnitude in Europe and the US. We do not find clear evidence that industry-level AI adoption is associated with employment changes. We discuss limitations of existing data and outline priorities for future data collection to better assess the productivity and labor market effects of AI.

title: Inference on Cross-Sectional Fit in Linear Factor Models
affiliations: University of Miami - School of Business Administration - Department of Economics, Hanken School of Economics - Department of Finance and Statistics, Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Mathematical Sciences and Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) - Department of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Inference on Cross-Sectional Fit in Linear Factor Models
detail.abstract: This paper develops inference for a cross-sectional R^2 constructed from estimated intercepts in multivariate time-series regressions and for differences in this measure across competing linear factor models. In traded-factor asset pricing, the statistic measures the fraction of cross-sectional dispersion in mean returns explained by the model. We show that its asymptotic behavior is regime dependent: under interior configurations it is T^0.5-Gaussian with feasible HAC variance estimation, whereas at perfect fit and related boundary cases it is nonregular and converges at rate T to quadratic-form limits. We develop feasible inference for each regime and comparison tests for nested and non-nested models. Simulations and empirical applications show that apparent differences in model fit often reflect substantial sampling uncertainty.

title: AURA Policy Uncertainty Index: A Real-Time, Market-Implied Index Constructed from Prediction Market Prices
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AURA Policy Uncertainty Index: A Real-Time, Market-Implied Index Constructed from Prediction Market Prices
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the AURA Policy Uncertainty Index (AURA-PUI), a continuous, market-implied measure of U.S. political and policy uncertainty derived from binary and multi-outcome prediction market contracts traded on regulated and established platforms. Unlike text-based measures such as the Baker-Bloom-Davis Economic Policy Uncertainty Index, the AURA-PUI captures revealed preferences (the actual positioning of capital under real financial consequences) rather than media sentiment proxies. The methodology employs a Fisher Information Score computed natively in logit space as the primary uncertainty measure, combined with bid-ask-adjusted logit-space volatility to distinguish active from stale uncertainty. Contracts are weighted by a composite of trading volume, bid-ask spread, and quantitative economic salience, with layered concentration constraints and correlation screening to prevent redundant clustering. The index publishes continuously on a 24/7 schedule with daily primary snapshots and hourly indicative values. A dual-series architecture provides both a fully replicable benchmark series (AURA-PUI-L, liquidity-only weights) and an enhanced series incorporating economically-motivated salience overlay. The AURA-PUI-L benchmark series is specified with all free parameters, theoretical justifications, and reconstitution rules sufficient for independent replication.

title: Procedural Asymmetry in News Coverage Inference Thresholds, Attribution Tempo, and Institutional Risk in Matched Media Events

detail.title: Procedural Asymmetry in News Coverage Inference Thresholds, Attribution Tempo, and Institutional Risk in Matched Media Events

declarations.declarationOfInterest: A view from an Ordinary Joe

detail.abstract:
Modern news institutions frequently apply uneven levels of causal attribution, identity emphasis, and evidentiary certainty to otherwise comparable events. Similar fact patterns—such as lone-actor violence, protest disorder, or institutional misconduct—often receive different reporting tempos and narrative constraints depending on the perceived social status of the actors involved. This paper models those differences as institutional behaviors rather than ideological choices.

I introduce two core concepts. An asymmetric permission structure describes the socially mediated reputational incentives that govern which actors can be criticized or speculated about with minimal professional risk. Directional evidentiary thresholds describe the variable quantity and quality of evidence required before institutions feel permitted to assign causal or ideological attribution. Together, these mechanisms predict that attribution will be faster and based on thinner evidence in some directions, and slower and more evidentially demanding in others. In contrast to law, which formalizes burdens and standards of proof, media decision-making operates with informal, status-contingent thresholds that emerge from reputational risk management rather than explicit doctrine.

The paper advances a typology of burden-shifting events—fact patterns that are materially similar across cases and therefore function as diagnostic tests for procedural symmetry. Using a small, hand-coded pilot sample of matched events (selected on crime type, scale, and timing), I compare attribution tempo, identity foregrounding, evidentiary language, and headline framing. The pilot coding reveals consistent differences in how quickly group-level explanations are permitted, how much evidence is required, and how cautiously identity is treated, even under comparable factual conditions. Inter-coder agreement measures are reported to ensure baseline reliability.

The argument does not allege coordinated bias or bad faith by individual journalists. Instead, it interprets asymmetric reporting as an emergent property of institutional risk optimization: organizations minimize reputational and liability exposure, and uneven evidentiary standards follow predictably. When attribution thresholds vary by actor status rather than fact pattern, institutions risk substituting defensive caution for epistemic consistency, with downstream consequences for public trust and perceived legitimacy.

By reframing contested "media bias" debates as questions of procedural symmetry and burden allocation, the paper offers a structural account of variation in coverage. That account is portable across domains and testable with future empirical work.

title: Can't Shake It Off: Earthquakes and Social Cohesion in Italy
affiliations: GSSI, Gran Sasso Science Institute, Gran Sasso Science Institute (GSSI) and Gran Sasso Science Institute (GSSI)

detail.title: Can't Shake It Off: Earthquakes and Social Cohesion in Italy
detail.abstract: Do earthquakes strengthen social cohesion or undermine it? While some theories suggest they strengthen social bonds, others suggest they lead to social disintegration. We add to the limited causal evidence on this phenomenon using the 2012 Northern Italy earthquake, and exploit a unique dataset that captures different earthquake characteristics and multiple dimensions of social cohesion through behavioral measures. Difference-in-differences and event-study estimates show that the earthquake shifted behavior toward individualism and out-group hostility, and that short-run increases in linking social capital were followed by later erosion. Critically, dwelling damage had stronger and more persistent effects than the physical shaking, suggesting that visible, measurable destruction has a more profound impact on social cohesion. These findings further advance our understanding by demonstrating that different dimensions of social cohesion respond differently to earthquakes, with varying recovery patterns depending on earthquake characteristics.

title: Political Determinants of the News Market: Novel Data and Quasi-Experimental Evidence from India
affiliations: ,  and University of Oslo, NUPI - Norwegian Institute for International Affairs

detail.title: Political Determinants of the News Market: Novel Data and Quasi-Experimental Evidence from India
detail.abstract: Information conveyed through news media influences political behavior. But to what extent are media markets themselves shaped by political determinants? We build a novel panel dataset of newspaper markets in India from 2002 to 2017 to measure the impact of changes in apportionment on the development of the news industry over time. We exploit the announcement of an exogenous change in the boundaries of electoral constituencies (the 2008 delimitation) to causally identify the relationship between the (future) apportionment of news markets and the change in the number and circulation of newspapers. Using an event-study model and a staggered Difference-in-Differences approach, we show that markets that faced an increase in representation experienced a significant rise in both circulation and the number of titles per capita. News and current affairs newspapers respond more to this increase. Furthermore, we document various dimensions of heterogeneity and show in particular that the magnitude of the estimated effects is larger in places with a relatively low level of newspaper and political competition prior to the 2008 delimitation.

title: Growing the Civic Mind: Civic Education, Civic Behavior, and Political Institutions
affiliations: University of Lausanne

detail.title: Growing the Civic Mind: Civic Education, Civic Behavior, and Political Institutions
detail.abstract: Declining civic engagement increasingly strains welfare state institutions. This paper asks whether civic values can be shaped through early educational investments. I study Tax and School, a large-scale program implemented in Italian primary and secondary schools to promote fiscal and civic responsibility. Exploiting staggered cross-municipality adoption, I find that exposure increases students' intrinsic motivation for rule compliance and reduces antisocial behaviors, particularly in socio-economically disadvantaged contexts. These student-level responses gradually aggregate into community-level outcomes: exposed municipalities later exhibit higher voter turnout and stronger support for redistributive policies. Survey evidence points to belief updating about the value of public goods and the role of government in mitigating inequality as a central mechanism. Counterfactual simulations imply that scaling the program could attenuate the secular decline in voter turnout.

title: Electoral Politics, Institutional Strain, And The Trajectory Of Constitutional Democracy In India
affiliations: ,  and Aligarh Muslim University Aligarh

detail.title: Electoral Politics, Institutional Strain, And The Trajectory Of Constitutional Democracy In India
detail.abstract: India, the world's largest constitutional democracy, represents a distinctive constitutional experiment combining parliamentary governance, federal distribution of powers, entrenched fundamental rights, and an activist judiciary. While the continuity of elections and peaceful transfer of power remain intact, contemporary developments have generated scholarly debate regarding the quality and trajectory of Indian constitutional democracy. This paper examines whether structural features such as the First-Past-the-Post electoral system, executive centralisation, politicisation of constitutional bodies, expansion of identity-based mobilisation, and digital transformation of political communication reflect democratic consolidation or incremental institutional strain. Adopting doctrinal constitutional analysis, comparative democratic theory, and jurisprudential evaluation of landmark decisions including Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, this study situates India within global scholarship on democratic backsliding. It argues that while India's constitutional architecture remains structurally robust-particularly due to the Basic Structure doctrine and judicial review-the resilience of democracy depends upon institutional culture, transparency in political funding, federal balance, and adherence to constitutional morality. The paper concludes with institutional and procedural reform recommendations designed to strengthen democratic accountability while preserving constitutional pluralism.

title: Inflation Persistence in the SCO Countries: A Fractional Integration Approach
affiliations: Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Navarra - Department of Economics,  and Federal University of Technology Akure (FUTA)

detail.title: Inflation Persistence in the SCO Countries: A Fractional Integration Approach
detail.abstract: This paper uses fractional integration methods to analyse the long-memory and persistence properties of inflation in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) countries over the period from 1 January 1997 to 8 January 2025. This approach is more general than standard models based on the I(0) versus I(1) dichotomy, and is particularly suitable in the case of emerging countries such as the SCO ones, who have experienced structural change and different policy frameworks. Regardless of the assumption made about the errors in the model, the estimates of the fractional differencing parameter are found to imply unit root or explosive behaviour. This means that the effects of shocks tend to be long-lived, and thus decisive monetary policy actions appear to be required to bring inflation under control. Further, the subsample analysis suggests that the Russian invasion of Ukraine did not affect significantly the stochastic properties of the series under examination.

title: Him Too? Analyzing the Effects of Epstein Connections
affiliations: , Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School and University of Melbourne - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Him Too? Analyzing the Effects of Epstein Connections
detail.abstract: The Epstein files, released between September 2025 and January 2026, offer an unprecedented window into the social and professional network of a convicted sex offender whose ties extended deep into corporate America. We construct a comprehensive sample of all S&P 500 CEOs and board members serving between 2006 and 2026 - 52,266 unique individuals - and search the 1,293,753 text-bearing documents for evidence of their contact with Jeffrey Epstein. Using large language model (LLM) classification of 117,394 matched correspondences, we identify 67,637 that indicate direct contact with 1,179 S&P 500 CEOs or directors. We then document three main findings. First, firms whose CEOs or board members appeared in Epstein-related news coverage experienced significantly negative cumulative abnormal returns of up to -8.5% over a ten-day window following the January 30, 2026 DOJ release. Second, adding Epstein-mediated ties to the firm network increases overall density and reduces average path lengths significantly, meaning that Epstein effectively wired corporate America into a denser, more tightly interconnected governance network than would have existed otherwise. Third, we show that Epstein's network transmitted norm contagion through shared board connections. Firms with more Epstein-connected CEOs or directors exhibit significantly worse ESG outcomes: each additional connection is associated with approximately 2.3 more annual governance incidents and 4.0 more total incidents.

title: Homeownership and Aerosol Air Pollution
affiliations: Leipzig University and University of Leipzig

detail.title: Homeownership and Aerosol Air Pollution
detail.abstract: We show that particulate matter pollution is lower in advanced economies where political parties favor homeownership. We rationalize this with a simple model featuring a polluting industry and owner-occupiers who push to restrict undesirable land uses. Pollution declines when homeowners have enough political power to enforce their preferences. We test this using data from German planning regions (2002–2014). Exploiting World War II area bombing as an instrument for homeownership - via its long-run effects on tenure patterns - we provide evidence suggesting a causal link between higher homeownership rates and lower air pollution.

title: Reforming Fossil Fuel Subsidies with Citizens' Approval: The Case of Colombia
affiliations: , Universidad de los Andes, Colombia, , Universidad de los Andes, Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK), Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK) and

detail.title: Reforming Fossil Fuel Subsidies with Citizens' Approval: The Case of Colombia
detail.abstract: Subsidizing fossil fuel consumption is at odds with climate change mitigation and a heavy burden on public budgets. Yet, efforts to reform such subsidies often face strong public opposition. We examine whether informing citizens about the effects of fossil fuel subsidy reform (FFSR) and complementary policy measures can increase public acceptance. We study this question using a novel survey experiment in Colombia, a country currently aiming at reforming existing fossil fuel subsidies. Building on Hoy et al (2026), our experiment exposes respondents to different information treatments, including from an innovative calculation of personal costs, and options for complementary policy measures. Leveraging a representative sample with more than 3,600 respondents, we find that information provision alone has limited effects on public support, as citizens rarely update their - at times - incorrect beliefs. In contrast, policy design is crucial. Complementing FFSR with additional measures shifts public opinion from majority opposition to majority support. Informing about the environmental effects of FFSR is most effective and strongly increases support for environmentally oriented complementary policies. Opposition to FFSR without complementary measures remains primarily driven by concerns about impacts on poorer households.

title: The Effects of Perceived Ticker Familiarity on ETF Investment
affiliations: Louisiana State University, New Orleans and University of New Orleans - College of Business Administration

detail.title: The Effects of Perceived Ticker Familiarity on ETF Investment
detail.abstract: We investigate the link between ticker memorability and ETF investment from 1993 through 2023. Issuers often favor salient trading symbols for marketing reasons. Ticker symbol selection is non-random consistent with the strategic adoption of salient tickers to capture retail interest and justify higher fees. Using our familiarity proxies, we find ticker memorability is strongly associated with higher liquidity, idiosyncratic risk, expense ratio and retail ownership. Upgrades from non-memorable to memorable constitute the most common symbol change in our sample, exhibiting the largest post-change increases in liquidity and idiosyncratic risk. Results are robust to logit, fixed effects, correlated random effects, and difference-indifference estimations.

reference: International Journal for Educational and Vocational Guidance, 0[10.1007/s10775-026-09798-y]
title: Care as the Sine Qua Non: A Proposal for Situating an Ethic of Care Within the Social Justice Agenda of Career Development Research and Practice
affiliations: Griffith University - School of Psychology

detail.title: Care as the Sine Qua Non: A Proposal for Situating an Ethic of Care Within the Social Justice Agenda of Career Development Research and Practice

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal for Educational and Vocational Guidance, 0[10.1007/s10775-026-09798-y]

detail.abstract: This article proposes an 'integrative ethical lens' that positions care ethics as a bridge between social justice values and goals, addressing a key ethical gap to facilitate context-responsive research and practice actions. It critiques limitations of approaches underpinned solely by justice-ethics traditions, and building on the narrative turn, offers a pragmatic, action-focused framework grounded in the foundational elements of care. Foregrounding epistemic justice, the lens clarifies how social justice can be enacted through attuned career research and practice that are reimagined as ethical projects, where responsively attending to diverse voices and local knowledges is foundational to meaningful social justice.

title: How Effective are Energy Labels? Evidence from the 2021 EU Reform
affiliations: University of Warsaw, KU Leuven and University of Würzburg - Institute of Economics and Social Sciences

detail.title: How Effective are Energy Labels? Evidence from the 2021 EU Reform
detail.abstract: Energy labels are often used to promote the adoption of more energy-efficient domestic appliances. This paper provides evidence on the impact of the 2021 revision of the EU energy labeling regulation using product-level sales data on refrigerators in four European countries (Belgium, France, Germany, and Poland). We first document substantial cross-country differences in sales-weighted energy consumption, reflecting differences in product portfolios and consumer preferences. Controlling for product characteristics, average energy consumption declines by between 3.3% in France and 4.2% in Belgium following the reform. We subsequently estimate a product-level demand model that incorporates energy labels in utility either directly or through their associated 15-year electricity costs. The results indicate that consumers undervalue future energy costs under both labeling regimes, although the degree of undervaluation declines under the new labels. Counterfactual simulations suggest that the labeling reform generated only modest energy efficiency gains. Larger gains could be achieved through alternative policies: stricter minimum standards (banning the least efficient appliances) or fiscal incentives (a feebate scheme subsidizing efficient appliances while taxing inefficient ones).

title: The economics and psychology of carbon tax acceptance Evidence from a randomized survey experiment
affiliations: University of Oxford and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The economics and psychology of carbon tax acceptance Evidence from a randomized survey experiment
detail.abstract: The green transition faces multiple overlapping political economy challenges, with backlash against environmental policies driven both by economic concerns and politicization of climate change. We study how economic reasoning as well as social and psychological factors jointly shape public acceptance of carbon taxation (with uniform redistribution). Using a pre-registered survey experiment in the U.S. (N = 2, 688), we show that factual policy explanation and social norm-based video messages each increase short-run policy acceptance, but this does not translate into higher average environmental donations and, over time, effects on positive support become non-additional. However, combining the two interventions leads to a significant reduction in strong opposition to carbon taxation by over 20%. This effect persists for several months and is concentrated among Republicans and Independents. One potential mechanism for which we find evidence is that norm-based messaging causally reduces the perceived political bias of subsequent policy explanation. This is in line with the notion that, in polarized settings, factual information itself can become politicized.

title: Status of Women and Their Socio-economic and Internal Security Contribution  During Ottoman Period

detail.title: Status of Women and Their Socio-economic and Internal Security Contribution  During Ottoman Period

publicationDetails.detailsText: 6TH INTERNATIONAL ASSAM ISLAMIC UNION MODEL CONGRESS, Model ASRICA Confederation Public Order and Internal Security Organization, Volume 6, Pp.50-68

detail.abstract: The Ottoman Empire was one of history's most long-lived empires. It lasted for more than 600 years. The Ottoman Empire, at its peak, was Europe's, Africa's, and Western Asia's most remarkable ruling entity, encompassing a diverse variety of cultures, religions, and languages. Despite these contrasts, from 1299 through 1922, the empire thrived. Most of the Ottoman state's life affairs, security and economic and social activities were based on Islamic principles, rich in brotherhood, humanity, and ethics. So, can a state with Islamic principles deprive its women of society or it will give more rights than other political systems? There was little research on the role of women in Ottoman society until the 1970s. In the Ottoman Empire, women were often portrayed in the Harem, and this framework was repeatedly used to explain their lives. But the reality is much different. It is clear from the Ottoman archives that Ottoman women made a significant socioeconomic contribution to their families, communities and the state as well as contributed in internal security of the state by their involvement in security and intelligence. They also held the right to inheritance. Several instances illustrate that women in Anatolia were involved in trading and operating businesses. These illustrations prove that the Ottoman women were not deprived of justice and freedom, which is why they were freely able to contribute to society and state in all aspects. Apart from contribution to agriculture, animal husbandry, home economics, and textile production, the Ottoman women have made a noteworthy contribution to internal security directly or indirectly. This study highlights the importance of Ottoman women in social, economic, and interior security. It investigates the issues of women's property rights, the rights of inheritance, commerce, and participation in state and regional security and intelligence by referring to current research and literature.

title: Coherent Collective Cognition (CCC): A System-of-Systems Architecture with Design Specifications, Operational Validation and Backward Interpretation
affiliations: The Force Global Research Facility

detail.title: Coherent Collective Cognition (CCC): A System-of-Systems Architecture with Design Specifications, Operational Validation and Backward Interpretation
detail.abstract: This article specifies and validates an invariant-constrained recursive coherence architecture for collective intelligence under increasing complexity. Contemporary systems fail structurally due to absence of invariant admissibility constraints and identity continuity. The Bounded Creativity Syndicate (BCS) architecture resolves this through Nano-Net invariant geometry, Forum-mediated distributed validation, and Recursive Identity Maintenance (RIM), enforcing coherence preservation (ΔC_t ≥ 0) and normalized recursive state balance (C_t + L_t + D_t = 1). Operational validation (BCS 2.0) demonstrates the first Collective Cognitive Capability governed by invariant geometry rather than centralized control or consensus. A six-layer architecture extends coherence from system to civilizational scale as a falsifiable proposition, validated through RED ZONE replication and BLUE ZONE stabilization. Complete invariant specification enables independent replication and evaluation, transforming coherence preservation into a mathematically anchored, empirically validated recursive intelligence architecture.

title: You Can't Always Get What You Want (Where You Want It): Cross-Border Effects of the US Money Market Fund Reform
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: You Can't Always Get What You Want (Where You Want It): Cross-Border Effects of the US Money Market Fund Reform
detail.abstract: This paper documents significant cross-border effects of the 2014 US money market fund (MMF) reform on euro area MMFs. As US-based prime funds became less money-like due to the reform, euro area-based prime funds received large inflows from foreign investors. These cross-border flows were motivated by the search for stable NAV instruments. Consistent with an easing of competitive pressure, euro area prime MMFs reduced their risk-taking. Lastly, the EU MMF regulation, a weaker regulatory intervention compared to the US reform, did not lead to a reversal of the documented cross-border flows.

title: The US Taxpayer Harm Test: An Emerging Basis for Extraterritorial Antitrust Enforcement in the Shadow of Law

detail.title: The US Taxpayer Harm Test: An Emerging Basis for Extraterritorial Antitrust Enforcement in the Shadow of Law
detail.abstract: This article examines the emergence, development and implications of the taxpayer harm test as a novel jurisdictional basis in United States antitrust enforcement. Developed entirely through agency practice, without legislative or judicial grounding, it extends the extraterritorial reach of US law to anticompetitive conduct abroad where foreign transactions are substantially funded by the US government. Unlike the effects doctrine, which grounds jurisdiction in competitive harm within the forum market, the taxpayer harm test relies on fiscal injury to the US treasury, and by extension its taxpayers. The article traces the origins of the test in agency guidelines and early cases, including US military procurement abroad, its recognition in the 1995 and 2017 Guidelines, and its application in recent enforcement actions. It shows how the test has been used to support expansive assertions while avoiding judicial scrutiny at home. The article highlights the absence of legislative mandate or judicial endorsement, and assesses the test’s compatibility with established principles of jurisdiction under international law. It argues that while the test advances US enforcement goals and strengthens deterrence, it stretches extraterritoriality beyond recognized limits. By analysing this unexplored doctrine, the article contributes to wider debates on unilateral innovation in competition law and the governance of cross-border economic activity.

title: After the FTC Noncompete Rule
affiliations: Loyola University Chicago School of Law

detail.title: After the FTC Noncompete Rule

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author served as a Senior Adviser to the Federal Trade Commission in 2022 and worked on certain matters relating to the topic of this article. This article represents only the personal opinions of the author and is based solely on publicly available information.
declarations.funderStatement: The author has received only a summer research grant and research assistance paid by his employer Loyola University Chicago School of Law.

detail.abstract:
Noncompete clauses in employment agreements are pervasive in the United States. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) estimated that 20% or more of all workers in the United States are covered by such agreements.

The study of noncompete clauses has remained largely siloed. This essay seeks to bridge that gap by looking at noncompete clauses as a holistic issue that harms workers and the economy regardless of the legal labels used to address the problem. I provide a taxonomy of the main approaches that currently exist and argue for the abolition of noncompete clauses moving forward on all fronts following the failure of the 2024 FTC rule to come into effect.

By highlighting the benefits of a comprehensive ban on noncompetes under each of the respective regulatory regimes, this essay identifies how a multi-faceted approach not only better protects workers but also limits unnecessarily broad exceptions that have developed over time. I argue that noncompete clauses harm workers by limiting their bargaining power at their present jobs and prevents them from pursuing the most likely next jobs that will better their lives. Society at large is also harmed the prevalence of noncompetes because of the loss of new companies, innovation, and competition through the restrictions on entrepreneurship when a worker wants to strike out on their own or join a competing venture.

Firms do have legitimate interests to protect, but not to the degree they frequently assert. The firms also have numerous less restrictive options in most cases to protect those legitimate interests ranging from less draconian agreements to simply treating their workers better.

In the event that a total ban is not politically feasible, I suggest four improvements to the current patchwork approaches at the state level including: 1) a narrow “C-Suite exception” in lieu of the more common existing salary cap exceptions; 2) banning noncompetes for all workers and not just traditional employees; 3) banning other post-employment restrictions that amount to “defacto” noncompetes; and 4) creating procedural protections including advance notice, cooling off periods, and burdens of proof on employers seeking to enforce noncompete obligations.

title: The Labor Market Returns to Delaying Pregnancy
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago,  and

detail.title: The Labor Market Returns to Delaying Pregnancy
detail.abstract: We study the labor market impact of unplanned pregnancy among women using long-acting reversible contraceptives to delay pregnancy. While most women successfully delay, some have unplanned pregnancies, providing quasi-random variation in pregnancy timing. Analyzing linked health and labor market data from Sweden, we find that unplanned pregnancies halt women's career progression, resulting in income losses of 19% five years later. We find similar effects of unplanned births among women using short-acting reversible contraceptives. Using pregnancy as an instrument for birth in a dynamic treatment effect framework, effects of unplanned children are more detrimental for younger women and those enrolled in education.

title: Special Education Substantially Improves Learning: Evidence from Three States
affiliations: Saint Anselm College, , Biden School of Public Policy & Administration, University of Delaware, , Boston University, Wheelock College of Education and Human Development and Boston University

detail.title: Special Education Substantially Improves Learning: Evidence from Three States
detail.abstract: Special education serves more than one in seven U.S. students yet its causal impact remains understudied. Using longitudinal data from Massachusetts, Indiana, and Connecticut, we estimate the effect of individualized supports with an event-study design that tracks achievement around initial classification. Students' scores decline prior to placement and rise sharply afterward, yielding a consistent V-shaped pattern. Within three years, achievement is 0.2–0.4σ higher than counterfactual trends imply. Gains are similar across disability categories and subgroups, are not driven by testing accommodations, and remain under conservative assumptions. Individualized supports substantially increase learning productivity.

title: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Local Economic Effects of Data Center Entry

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The explosive growth of artificial intelligence has triggered an unprecedented wave of data center investment, yet systematic evidence on how these facilities affect local economies remains scarce. We study the local economic effects of data center entry in the United States using comprehensive facility-level data merged with county-level economic outcomes. Employing a Callaway-Sant'Anna difference-in-differences framework that accounts for staggered treatment timing, we find that data center activation increases local employment by 3.5%, total wages by 5.0%, business establishments by 4.7%, and median household income by 1.9%, while reducing unemployment rates and stimulating building permit activity. These effects are concentrated in metropolitan areas, where agglomeration economies amplify multiplier effects, while non-metro counties experience negligible gains. Big Tech facilities generate larger effects than third-party data centers, and counties with early first-entry timing experienced stronger effects than those with recent first-entry timing. We also find that counties receiving additional data centers within five years of first entry exhibit larger effects than counties with isolated entries, suggesting that data center clustering amplifies local economic benefits. Finally, we examine electricity price effects, finding that identification is complicated by utility service territories spanning multiple counties. In areas with cleaner identification (fewer shared utilities), we detect positive price effects, suggesting data center demand raises costs for local ratepayers. Our findings inform ongoing policy debates about data center expansion and its local economic consequences.

title: Accounting-based Debt Covenants and Lenders' Private Information: Theory and Evidence from Global Air Connectivity

detail.title: Accounting-based Debt Covenants and Lenders' Private Information: Theory and Evidence from Global Air Connectivity
detail.abstract: This study provides a theoretical and empirical analysis of how loan contracts are designed when accounting-based covenants contingently allocate control rights, and lenders engage in costly private information acquisition following covenant violations. The benefit of lenders' private information acquisition is greater when accounting signals are less informative about efficient liquidations. We show that optimal debt contracts set tighter covenants and lower interest spreads when lenders' marginal private information acquisition costs are lower. Furthermore, both effects are stronger for borrowers with lower accounting information quality. Using syndicated loan data, we test these predictions by exploiting global long-distance passenger air links as a proxy for information acquisition costs and find results consistent with the model. We further strengthen our identification by employing a regression discontinuity approach based on the discontinuity of direct flight availability around 6,000 miles. Placebo tests using cargo flights and flights to participant lenders show no significance, confirming the private information acquisition by lead lenders in syndicated loans.

title: Empowering Women in the Green Transition: Bridging Policy Gaps in Vocational Training and Upskilling in India

detail.title: Empowering Women in the Green Transition: Bridging Policy Gaps in Vocational Training and Upskilling in India
detail.abstract: India stands at a critical juncture: its ambitious renewable energy agenda promises millions of new green jobs, yet the policies and infrastructure designed to build this workforce have largely failed to account for gender. Women, who constitute only a marginal fraction of India's renewable energy workforce, face a compounding set of structural, socio-cultural, and logistical barriers that existing vocational training frameworks have not adequately addressed. This paper conducts a secondary policy analysis of India's current green skills ecosystem-examining flagship schemes such as Skill India and the Skill Council for Green Jobs-against the backdrop of international frameworks on gender-just transitions advanced by the ILO, UN Women, UNIDO, and IRENA. Drawing on a targeted review of policy documents, institutional reports, and existing field research, this paper identifies three dominant themes: a severe skills mismatch between projected green job creation and women's training access; deep structural barriers including unsafe transport, unpaid care burdens, and restrictive gender norms; and an absence of gender-intentional design in existing government schemes. The paper proposes four actionable policy recommendations-mandated gender quotas and targeted funding in green skills programs, decentralized community-level training infrastructure, integrated financial stipends and childcare support, and a gender-responsive monitoring and evaluation framework. The central argument is that achieving India's climate commitments and a true Just Transition is not merely a matter of environmental policy, but demands aggressive, gender-intentional workforce development as a foundational pillar.

title: Predictive Factor Model for Jump Intensities

detail.title: Predictive Factor Model for Jump Intensities
detail.abstract: We propose a parsimonious factor model for jump intensities for a large number of stocks, which we call the Jump Factor Intensity Thinning (J-FIT) Model. The model utilizes a jump factor process to capture the complete grid of potential jumps, and a thinning procedure to capture individual stock jumps. The jump factor process features temporal dependence, which leads to predictability. We develop estimators and inference theories for the model parameters, enabling applications such as jump intensity prediction and constructing prediction intervals for the jump risk exposures of individual stocks and sectors. Empirically, we provide solid evidence that jumps are predictable with the J-FIT model, whose predictive performance substantially sur- passes various benchmark models. We also demonstrate that J-FIT is useful for tail risk management.

title: Across the Grid: How Generation Entry Shapes Congestion and Locational Price Dispersion

detail.title: Across the Grid: How Generation Entry Shapes Congestion and Locational Price Dispersion
detail.abstract: This paper studies how generation entry reshapes the spatial distribution of congestion prices across the transmission network. When generation enters a network, new electricity flows can create location-specific congestion prices, generating spatially uneven price impacts across locations. We propose a differences-indifferences design that addresses identification challenges arising from network-wide spillovers and apply this framework to high-frequency nodal data from the PJM electricity market. We find that the distributional consequences of generation entry vary by generator type: wind entry increases congestion prices mainly in areas where fossil-fuel plants operate, while natural gas plant entry has no significant impact. These contrasting results indicate that generator characteristics, such as dispatchability, along with network structure are critical determinants of the spatial distribution of consumer costs and generator rents following capacity additions.
