detail.abstract: For seventy years, international relations theory shared a quiet assumption: that states are coherent enough to choose. Kantian Event Horizon Theory (KEHT) tests that assumption against 3,281 country-year observations across 176 countries from 2006 to 2024-and finds that it describes approximately 59% of the post 2006 international system. The other 41% operates below a critical coherence threshold where the behavioral predictions of standard IR theory systematically invert or fail.

title: The Intelligence Yield Curve: A Quantitative Framework for Measuring How Intelligence Compounding Drives Enterprise Value

detail.title: The Intelligence Yield Curve: A Quantitative Framework for Measuring How Intelligence Compounding Drives Enterprise Value
detail.abstract: AI startups captured between 50% and 61% of global venture capital in 2025 (OECD; Crunchbase; PitchBook), yet fewer than 1% of companies have achieved advanced AI maturity as measured by structured assessment (ServiceNow Enterprise AI Maturity Index, 2025). The gap between perceived and actual intelligence capability creates systematic mispricing. Investors lack a quantitative tool to separate companies that compound intelligence from those that merely rent it, to identify where intelligence is stuck within a portfolio company, and to track the trajectory of intelligence maturity as a board-level metric alongside ROIC and EBITDA. This paper introduces the Intelligence Yield Curve TM (IYC), a framework that bridges this gap by quantifying the rate at which a company compounds intelligence from its own data and connecting that rate directly to enterprise valuation. The framework produces a single coefficient, beta (the Intelligence Yield Coefficient TM), derived from a scored diagnostic across five dimensions of intelligence maturity: Data Depth, Intelligence Reinforcement, Feedback Frequency, Human-AI Integration, and Adoption Breadth. Beta maps to implied EV/Revenue multiples and forward compounding projections using a formula structure that deliberately parallels the Capital Asset Pricing Model. The formula structure implies that small increases in beta produce disproportionate enterprise value expansion due to compounding effects. At the default calibration (k=1.0, alpha=1.2), the mapping produces implied EV/Revenue multiples ranging from 1.5x at the floor to 15.0x at the ceiling, consistent with the spread observed in B2B technology valuations at Series A through growth stage. Unlike existing AI maturity frameworks, which assess operational readiness without financial linkage, the IYC provides investors and boards with a measurable, trackable intelligence variable that drives enterprise value estimation and targeted operational intervention. The full scored diagnostic instrument is maintained as a proprietary assessment tool.

title: Uncivil Wars: Does Kantian Adaptive Networks Theory Provide Significant Indications and Warning of Intra-State

detail.title: Uncivil Wars: Does Kantian Adaptive Networks Theory Provide Significant Indications and Warning of Intra-State
detail.abstract:
Can the breakdown of the "Kantian Tripod" predict the onset of civil war? Building on the work of Russett and Oneal (2001), this research develops Kantian Adaptive Networks Theory to provide a mathematical framework for the Indications and Warning (I&W) of intra-state conflict.

Utilizing a set of longitudinal data (2005-2013) from the Fragile States Index (FSI) and the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP), this study employs regression and Vector Autoregression (VAR) models to isolate specific institutional decays—the "Mincemeat" precursors—that precede state collapse. Through comparative case studies of Kenya and Syria, the research demonstrates how social, economic, and political pressures induce network effects that transition states into active conflict.

Chaired by John Gerring at Boston University, this study serves as the empirical foundation for the Mincemeat Differential ($\Phi$). It bridges the gap between traditional International Relations theory and operational strategic intelligence, offering a surgical approach to conflict prediction that identifies the systemic vulnerabilities preceding a state's descent into "Uncivil War."

title: The News-Contaminated Market: Local Factors and Asset Pricing

detail.title: The News-Contaminated Market: Local Factors and Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Much of the information arriving in financial markets has a local structure: It directly affects subsets of firms while also generating a market-wide effect. Observationally, this can be modeled as a factor structure with a global factor and local factors that need not be orthogonal to each other. Because the value-weighted market factor aggregates both components, it conflates the global factor with the local components, giving rise to the news-contaminated market. We propose a decomposition of the market factor into a global component and an orthogonal residual, the local news factor (LNF), leveraging high-frequency data to capture the time-varying factor structure. Under this decomposition, market beta reflects exposure to both global and local components, giving rise to an omitted variable bias in beta-sorted portfolios. This bias flattens the security market line (SML), as the raw local factors are negatively correlated with the global factor, while the residual LNF is only weakly priced. In particular, the LNF is strongly priced overnight but exhibits excess volatility and negative returns during the day. Controlling for local exposures restores an upward-sloping SML, even during intraday periods and non-special days when the SML is particularly flat. The two-factor decomposition helps span low-risk anomalies, including betting-against-beta and idiosyncratic volatility, and explains the shrinking beta dispersion during the trading day. Together, these findings identify the contamination of the market factor by local news shocks as a common source of the flat SML, low-risk anomalies, and intraday beta dynamics.

title: Architectural Scope:Supra-Ecosystem Institutional Architecture and the Logic of Digital Diversification
affiliations: Shih Chien University - Department of Marketing Management and Yuan Ze University

detail.title: Architectural Scope:Supra-Ecosystem Institutional Architecture and the Logic of Digital Diversification
detail.abstract: The digital age has fundamentally reconfigured the logic of corporate diversification. Firms such as Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Tesla have successfully diversified into seemingly unrelated industries — not through traditional relatedness in assets or operations, but through shared data infrastructure, API protocols, and governance architectures. Yet prevailing diversification theory, grounded in asset redeployment, economies of scope, and M-form coordination, lacks the conceptual vocabulary to explain this new logic of scope.This paper develops Supra-Ecosystem Institutional Architecture (SIA) theory — a formal framework that reconceptualizes digital diversification as a process of architectural scope rather than product-market scope. We introduce the supra-ecosystem as the analytical level at which digital diversifiers govern multi-domain portfolios: an overlapping space of multiple innovation ecosystems where cross-domain coordination occurs without a single orchestrating actor. We theorize SIA as constituted by three generative mechanisms — structural coupling, governance interfaces, and legitimacy alignment — and develop a three-layer institutional ontology linking institutional logics, institutional architecture, and contextualized agency.SIA theory redefines corporate relatedness as architectural relatedness: the degree to which formerly unrelated domains are structurally coupled through shared data infrastructure and governance protocols. It provides the institutional logic of the emerging CM-form (centralized multidivisional form): architectural centrality over data and AI infrastructure enables decentralized market execution because governance is embedded in technical interfaces rather than managerial hierarchies. Five cross-domain propositions and illustrative vignettes spanning industrial AI, digital health, global payments, electromobility-energy coupling, and transnational vaccine governance demonstrate the theory's explanatory reach.

detail.abstract: I study how AI adoption can undermine prediction markets through an endogenous adverse-selection spiral. When AI raises the informational advantage of some traders, market makers widen spreads, pricing out uninformed participants whose exit further concentrates informed order flow. In the model, beyond a critical AI penetration threshold no active equilibrium survives. Under a participation-based welfare criterion, AI adoption can reduce trading surplus and may be privately excessive because adopters ignore the participation externality they impose. Moreover, the collapse destroys not only trading surplus but also the market's capacity to generate informative public prices---its core social function---so that even a planner who values only price informativeness would find unchecked AI adoption suboptimal. The mechanism extends to imperfect AI, heterogeneous quality, reduced-form dynamics, automated market makers, multi-market environments, and richer distributions of predictive ability.

title: Internal Governance Monopoly: A Working Concept for Structural Failure in Modern Organizations

detail.title: Internal Governance Monopoly: A Working Concept for Structural Failure in Modern Organizations
detail.abstract:
Most organizations do not fail because people stop trying or leaders stop caring about the work. They fail because too much decision authority ends up within the same organizational structure, usually the same office, the same department or the same role. These condensed structures decide what matters, what gets tracked and what is reported both internally and externally. Work that should be handled across the organization keeps landing in the same narrow lane. This results in slowed decisions, extra work, and ultimately burnout or migration. Exceptional staff and leaders leave while the organization treats that as a staffing or execution problem. However, it is the structure of the organization itself that produces that strain.

Internal governance monopoly is the name used for that condition. It exists when too much authority inside an organization is concentrated in one part of the structure. This begins shaping the work far beyond what is appropriate or efficient. Once that happens, the organization creates extra work just to keep functioning in the same manner. Issues that should be handled directly must be translated first. Requests are rerouted through the default lane while delays continue to accrue. A perpetually increasing amount of work depends on the same few players to keep the organization moving.

Public agencies, nonprofits and firms all develop this pattern. Financial dominance is the most common form because finance predominantly holds formal authority both inside and outside the organization. However, finance is not the problem. They are partners within the same organization at odds due to a convergence of power that should not exist. Finance is forced to carry decisions and reporting burdens that should not have landed there in the first place. The deeper problem is that the kinds of work and value that were never given standing end up being passed through and being translated by finance in order to count. Burnout, turnover, rework and chronic overload usually start within this concentrated organizational structure. Capacity, coordination and execution are all impacted. The problem is getting harder to overlook as reporting demands continue to widen and AI increases pressure on organizations to produce clear evidence. This paper introduces internal governance monopoly as a working concept for naming the problem and building a better way to structure internal organizational authority.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how AI access changes market quality. In a noisy rationalexpectations model with hedging motives, exclusive AI creates private informational rents, worsens adverse selection, and can raise price impact when adoption is limited. Broad access instead compresses informational asymmetry and can restore risk sharing. I solve the exclusive regime in closed form, show that price informativeness is exactly quadratic in adoption, and derive conditions under which liquidity and welfare recover at high adoption. Market quality is therefore nonmonotonic in AI diffusion, and intermediate exclusive access can be dominated by the endpoints. A sharp threshold on common-signal precision determines whether the socially preferred endpoint is democratized access or universal private adoption.

Using a simple model of expected domesticwelfare, we show that a marginal increase in rare earth elementimports generates both private costs and social costs that are notconsidered in import decisions. title: Business Intelligence as a Differentiated Decision-Support Capability: A Multi-Level Analysis of SMEs' Decision-Making Quality

detail.title: Business Intelligence as a Differentiated Decision-Support Capability: A Multi-Level Analysis of SMEs' Decision-Making Quality
detail.abstract: While Business Intelligence (BI) is widely adopted, evidence regarding its differentiated value across managerial levels-particularly in resource-constrained small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)-remains fragmented (Zamani et al., 2017; Llave, 2019). This study investigates how BI utilization at strategic, tactical, and operational levels is associated with perceived decisionmaking quality (DMQ). A quantitative, cross-sectional survey of 186 SME managers in SMEs located in Kent, Southeast England, was analysed using exploratory factor analysis and multiple regression on standardised construct scores. Results reveal that BI utilization is positively associated with DMQ across all levels, but the impact is not uniform. Operational BI demonstrates the strongest association (β = .364, p < .001), followed by strategic (β = .267, p < .001) and tactical BI (β = .259, p = .001), collectively explaining 63.4% of the variance in DMQ. These findings suggest that in SME settings, operational applications deliver the most immediate decision benefits. By disaggregating BI across managerial levels, this study refines the understanding of BI as a differentiated decision-support capability rather than a homogeneous resource (Popovič et al., 2012). The results offer practical guidance for SMEs to prioritize and align BI investments with decision-specific requirements under resource constraints.

title: Financial Judicial Specialization and Bond Risk Pricing: Evidence from China's Financial Courts

detail.title: Financial Judicial Specialization and Bond Risk Pricing: Evidence from China's Financial Courts
detail.abstract: This study exploits the establishment of city-level financial courts in China as an exogenous shock to examine how financial judicial specialization affects bond risk pricing. Using firm-level bond issuance data from 2007–2023, we find that financial courts significantly compress local firms’ bond credit spreads through three channels: stronger ex-ante deterrence, higher judicial efficiency, and improved information disclosure quality. The effect is more pronounced for lower-rated bonds, non–state-owned enterprises, firms with low analyst coverage, and regions with weaker financial development and regulation. Beyond pricing effects, financial courts also expand firms’ bond financing scale and promote corporate investment. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of legal enforcement in bond market valuation.

detail.abstract: Online search engines depend on external content to respond to user queries, while content providers rely on search engines for visibility and user acquisition. The integration of GenAI-based summaries into search interfaces (eg, Google's AI Overviews (AIOs)) may reduce users' incentives to visit downstream publishers. Despite growing regulatory and industry attention, causal evidence on the effects of AI-generated summaries on search behavior remains limited. This paper provides causal evidence on the impact of AIOs on user behavior and downstream engagement using a field experiment that randomly assigns users to either the standard Google Search experience with AIOs or a version where AIOs are removed. We develop a custom Chrome browser extension that passively tracks detailed browsing behavior while also enabling real-time modifications to the search engine results page (SERP), allowing us to precisely manipulate AIO exposure in a natural browsing environment. When they appear, AIOs reduce outbound organic clicks by 38% and increase the probability of a zero-click search by 33%. We find no effects on sponsored clicks or overall search frequency, implying that AIOs reduce total external traffic by lowering organic clicks per search. Heterogeneity analyses show that effects are concentrated when AIOs appear at the top of the page and among the highest-ranked organic results. Using survey evidence, we find that despite these behavioral effects, removing AIOs does not affect users' overall search experience, including perceived ease of finding information and the quality of results. Exploratory evidence from a third AI Mode condition, where users are redirected to a Gemini-powered conversational AI interface, suggests even stronger reductions in engagement with downstream publishers. Overall, the findings suggest that AIOs divert traffic away from publishers without delivering measurable improvements in user experience, raising important implications for competition policy, platform power, and publisher sustainability.

detail.title: The Global Variation in Risk and Time Preferences
detail.abstract: A growing body of empirical research has developed measures of economic preferences related to risk taking and intertemporal choice. This research has documented pronounced heterogeneity in preferences across and within societies, and also provided evidence that these differences are culturally transmitted. This chapter discusses existing data sets that allow for a comparable measurement across the globe, takes stock of commonalities and differences in approaches, and presents an extended synthetic cross-country data set that combines information from existing data sets. The analysis then establishes various empirical regularities, such as broadly similar patterns of heterogeneity across the globe, revealed by the different datasets, but also some systematic divergences by measurement approach, and substantial correlations of economic preferences with country-aggregate and individual-level outcomes and traits. We also briefly discuss international data sets measuring social preferences, and end with an outlook on avenues for future research.

title: The Original Ideas Game and the Vanishing of the Absurd Heroes: Academic Reputation Hierarchies and Their Implications

detail.title: The Original Ideas Game and the Vanishing of the Absurd Heroes: Academic Reputation Hierarchies and Their Implications
detail.abstract: In perfectly competitive academic and idea markets, a divide emerges between elite scientists and the rest. The elite publish original, impactful work, while others - absurd heroes - struggle for recognition, often in vain. Though the original ideas game produces an equilibrium resembling perfect competition, it is driven by a hierarchical structure. This reflects the organization of real-world science, where limited incentives and access prevent most researchers from publishing and advancing original ideas.

title: Prices and Immigration: A Firm Level Analysis

detail.title: Prices and Immigration: A Firm Level Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how immigration affects consumer prices. Using scanner data and instrumenting county-level immigration with historical ancestry patterns, we find that an inflow of 10,000 immigrants lowers four-year price growth by 0.58 percentage points. Leveraging variation in firm exposure through sales versus production locations, we show price declines stem entirely from the product demand channel: firms lower prices in response to immigrants in sales markets, not production locations. Evidence suggests that immigrants search more intensively, exhibit higher demand elasticity, pay lower prices for identical products, and shift expenditure toward lower-appeal products — consistent with a model of heterogeneous price sensitivity.

title: Unemployment Narratives
affiliations: ,  and University of Cologne

detail.title: Unemployment Narratives
detail.abstract: We study economic narratives - causal accounts of observed events - in a high-stakes real-world context: long-term unemployment. We use open-ended questions to measure narratives about long-term unemployment in samples of Danish unemployed job seekers, firm managers, households from the general population, and experts at labor market institutions, as well as international academic experts. We document three main results. First, there is pronounced heterogeneity in narratives both within and across samples. For instance, job seekers are more likely to attribute long-term unemployment to factors outside the control of the individual and less likely to attribute it to job seekers' own decisions than respondents in the other samples. Second, narratives strongly reflect job seekers' personal experiences during both the current and previous unemployment spells. Third, narratives shape job seekers' and firm managers' quantitative beliefs, decisions and labor market outcomes as measured in survey and linked administrative data, which we demonstrate in a field experiment and correlationally. Our findings highlight the experiential origins of economic narratives and underscore the key role of narratives in belief formation and decision making.
